findings.amendedDescription: src/components/AddBookModal.tsx advertises 'Maximum size: 10MB' at line 250 and enforces it nowhere — `handleFileChange` (lines 89-97) checks only `selected.type === 'application/pdf'`, `handleSubmit` (lines 50-87) has no size guard, and the submit button's disabled condition (lines 264-266) checks only loading state and file presence. A grep for `.size`/`1024`/`MAX_` across the add-book path returns no enforcement anywhere in the repo. A 500MB file is therefore accepted, expanded ~1.37x into a base64 data URL and posted to Gemini. Separately, `File.type` is browser-reported rather than content-sniffed, so a renamed file passes the MIME check. Re-scoped and downgraded to `low` as a type-safety finding: no assertion here claims PDF-ness (`file` is honestly `File | null`, and `StoredBlob.kind` at src/types.ts:71 is a store-slot discriminator used to build the `${bookId}:${kind}` primary key at src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126, not a claim about the bytes), so there is no lying type to fix. The proposed `ValidatedPdf` branded wrapper would have exactly one producer and one consumer and is not justified. The unenforced 10MB limit remains a genuine, cheap-to-fix robustness bug; the MIME-sniffing concern belongs to a security/validation audit.

findings.title: Unchecked-indexed-access cluster: 7 sites across the lot typed `string` where the runtime can yield `undefined`
findings.description: CLUSTER, reported once rather than seven times because the cause is a single tsconfig flag. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off, every array/regex index in these three files is typed as if it always hits. Sites: BookDetail.tsx:71 `headerMatch[1].length` and 72 `headerMatch[2]`; EReader.tsx:71 `(trimmed.match(/^#+/) || [''])[0].length`, 130 `const [num, ...rest] = trimmed.split('.')`, 141 `trimmed.charAt(0)`; ProfileView.tsx:80 `.map((n) => n[0])`. Every one of these is currently SAFE by construction - the regex groups are non-optional and guarded by a preceding `startsWith` test, `split` always returns at least one element, and `Array.prototype.join` stringifies `undefined` to `''` so `getInitials('')` yields `''` rather than throwing. They are listed as the migration cost of turning the flag on, not as live bugs. The one site in this lot that is a live bug is EReader.tsx:395 (L11-F07), which the same flag would have caught at the keystroke. FIX SHAPE: enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, fix EReader.tsx:395 properly, and satisfy these six with non-null-safe narrowing (`?? ''`, destructuring defaults) rather than `!`. Effort is small in this lot but the flag is repo-wide, so cost must be measured across all of `src` before enabling.
findings.verifierNote: The cluster is real but its enumeration is mostly wrong, and I measured this rather than reasoning about it. With `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess` the only errors in the three named files are BookDetail.tsx 71, 79 and 85. Of Discovery's seven claimed sites, six produce no error: EReader.tsx:141 `trimmed.charAt(0)` is a method call, not an index access at all; ProfileView.tsx:80 `n[0]` indexes a string, which the flag does not affect; EReader.tsx:130's destructure yields `string | undefined` for `num` but it is only rendered as a ReactNode at line 133, which accepts undefined; EReader.tsx:71 `(trimmed.match(/^#+/) || [''])[0].length` does not error because lib.es5 declares `RegExpMatchArray[0]: string`; and BookDetail.tsx:72 `const content = headerMatch[2]` is a legal assignment — the errors land downstream at 79 and 85 where content reaches formatInline. So the stated migration cost is overstated by roughly six of seven sites, and what remains is a strict subset of F109, which measured the flag correctly. The finding's core claim — that these sites are currently safe by construction, not live bugs — is accurate and worth keeping. Severity stays low.
findings.reachability: None as a defect; every listed site is safe by construction today, and six of them would not even require touching if the flag were enabled.
findings.blastRadius: 3 real sites (BookDetail.tsx 71, 79, 85), all already counted in F109's measured 10.
findings.suggestedPatch: Fold into F109. For the three real sites, destructure the match once: `const [, hashes, content] = headerMatch;` then `const level = hashes?.length ?? 0;` and pass `content ?? ''` at lines 79 and 85. Risk: none; no runtime change.
findings.amendedDescription: Unchecked-indexed-access illustration in BookDetail.tsx. Measured with the flag on, the only real sites in the three files named are BookDetail.tsx 71 (`headerMatch[1].length`), 79 and 85 (`content` reaching formatInline). The other sites originally listed — EReader.tsx 71/130/141 and ProfileView.tsx 80 — produce no error (charAt is not an index access, string indexing is unaffected by the flag, RegExpMatchArray declares element 0 as string, and a ReactNode accepts undefined). All three real sites are safe by construction and are already counted in F109's measured total of 10.

findings.title: Blob MIME type is a bare `string` carried from storage into `window.open` with no check
findings.description: `StoredBlob.type` is declared `string` (types.ts:79) and is whatever `blob.type` happened to be at upload (repo.ts:138). `blobs.get` reconstructs `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: record.type })` (repo.ts:144) - so the returned `Blob` carries an unvalidated MIME string that the type system says nothing about. BookDetail line 197-200 asks for the `'pdf'` blob and hands the resulting object URL to `window.open`. If the stored `type` is `''` (which happens for any `File` the browser could not sniff) or anything other than `application/pdf`, the browser does not render the PDF in a tab - it downloads it or opens a blank tab, and the 'Open Original PDF' button appears broken with no error. The `BlobKind` discriminator (`'pdf' | 'audio-short' | 'audio-long'`) is a proper literal union and IS correctly used at the call site, but it is not connected to the MIME string, so the two can disagree freely. VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the null path: `blobs.get` honestly returns `Blob | undefined` and line 198 handles it with an early return - no cast, no `!`. FIX SHAPE: type the MIME as a small literal union (or brand it) keyed off `BlobKind`, and set it from the kind rather than trusting the uploaded file's sniffed type. Separately worth noting (not a type finding): the object URLs created on lines 160 and 199 are never revoked, so each audio generation and each PDF open leaks a blob for the lifetime of the document.
findings.verifierNote: Verified: types.ts:79 declares `type: string`, repo.ts:138 stores whatever `blob.type` the browser derived from the picked File, repo.ts:144 replays it into the reconstructed Blob, and BookDetail.tsx:195-200 hands the resulting object URL to window.open. BlobKind is a proper literal union (types.ts:4) and is used correctly at the call site (`blobs.get(book.id, 'pdf')`, line 197) but is not connected to the MIME string, so the two can disagree with nothing to catch it. The `''` scenario is the plausible one: browsers derive File.type from the extension and normally yield application/pdf for .pdf, but an OS without the mapping registered yields '', after which window.open shows a blank tab or a download instead of a rendered PDF — a button that looks broken with no error surfaced. Note the migration path is safe because migrate.ts:137/143 hardcodes the MIME types. This is the consumer-side view of F114 and shares one fix; keeping it at low since the consequence here is UX rather than the origin concern.
findings.reachability: Add a book by PDF upload on a system where the browser reports an empty or non-PDF File.type, then click 'Open Original PDF' on the book detail page.
findings.blastRadius: 1 consumer (BookDetail.tsx:197-200); the shared origin is repo.ts:138.
findings.suggestedPatch: Same single change as F114 — derive the MIME from BlobKind in repo.ts (`type: MIME_BY_KIND[kind]` at line 138 and `{ type: MIME_BY_KIND[record.kind] }` at line 144) so blobs.get always returns a correctly-typed Blob. Risk: none; BookDetail needs no edit once the repo guarantees the type.

findings.title: `coverImageUrl: string` doubles as a "no cover" sentinel that only BookCard knows about; DailyWisdomModal renders it raw
findings.description: `Book.coverImageUrl` is typed `string` but carries out-of-band sentinel values for "no cover": the empty string, produced by the legacy migration (`legacy.coverImageUrl ?? ''`, migrate.ts:114), and — per BookCard's defensive check — the literal text `'null'`. BookCard is the only consumer that knows this: it substitutes a generated placeholder for both and installs an `onError` handler (BookCard.tsx:17-23, 57). DailyWisdomModal renders the value straight into `` with neither guard, so a migrated book with an empty cover produces ``, which browsers resolve to the current document URL — a request for the SPA's own HTML, decoded as an image, yielding a broken-image glyph inside the daily-wisdom card. BookDetail.tsx:241 has the same raw usage. The type is doing double duty (a URL *or* one of two absence markers) with no discriminator, which is why the knowledge of the sentinels lives in one component's `if` instead of in the type. Fix shape: make absence explicit — `coverImageUrl?: string` with a single shared `coverSrc(book)` helper that applies `placeholderCover` — so no consumer can forget. Blast radius: 3 render sites, 1 of which handles it.
findings.verifierNote: Verified on every leg. Book.coverImageUrl is `string` (types.ts:38) and carries two out-of-band absence markers: the empty string from migrate.ts:114 `coverImageUrl: legacy.coverImageUrl ?? ''`, and the literal 'null' that BookCard defends against. BookCard is indeed the only consumer that knows: BookCard.tsx:15-24 substitutes placeholderCover for `!book.coverImageUrl || book.coverImageUrl === 'null'` and line 57 installs onError. DailyWisdomModal.tsx:70-74 renders `src={book.coverImageUrl}` with neither guard nor onError, and BookDetail.tsx:240-244 does the same. An empty src resolves to the current document URL in every major browser, so the app requests its own HTML and decodes it as an image — a broken-image glyph inside the daily-wisdom card. Low is right: cosmetic, no crash, no data loss.
findings.reachability: Any migrated legacy book without a cover. AppShell.tsx:58-78 picks a random book for the daily-wisdom card, so such a book renders in DailyWisdomModal with an empty src; opening it renders the same empty src again at BookDetail.tsx:241.
findings.blastRadius: 1 producer of the sentinel (migrate.ts:114) and 3 consumers, of which only BookCard.tsx handles it.
findings.suggestedPatch: Extract BookCard's normalisation into src/lib/covers: `export const coverSrc = (url: string, title: string) => (!url || url === 'null' ? placeholderCover(title) : url);` and use it at DailyWisdomModal.tsx:71 and BookDetail.tsx:241, leaving BookCard's onError in place. Risk: none — pure function of the two values already in scope at both sites.

findings.title: `monthlyGoal: number` permits 0 and NaN, producing `strokeDasharray="NaN, 100"`
findings.description: `Profile.monthlyGoal` is a bare `number` (types.ts:21) where the domain is 'a positive integer'. Line 53 divides by it unguarded: `Math.min(100, (finishedCount / profile.monthlyGoal) * 100)`. A `monthlyGoal` of 0 makes the expression `Infinity` when any book is finished and `NaN` when none are, and line 209 then emits `strokeDasharray={`${NaN}, 100`}` - an invalid SVG attribute that the browser rejects with a console error and a mis-rendered progress ring. The write side is equally unbranded: line 239 stores `parseInt(e.target.value)`, whose TypeScript type is `number` but whose runtime range includes `NaN`. Reachability is low today - `profiles.create` defaults to 4 (repo.ts:21) and the range input is `min="1"` - but nothing prevents a 0 or a NaN arriving from the unvalidated backup import (L11-F04) or a migrated legacy record, and once written it is durable. FIX SHAPE: brand it as a positive integer validated at the repo boundary, or at minimum guard the division with a sensible floor at the read site.
findings.verifierNote: Verified. types.ts:21 `monthlyGoal: number`; ProfileView.tsx:53 `Math.min(100, (finishedCount / profile.monthlyGoal) * 100)` with no guard; ProfileView.tsx:209 `strokeDasharray={`${stats.progressPercent}, 100`}`; ProfileView.tsx:239 `monthlyGoal: parseInt(e.target.value)` on the range input. The arithmetic is as described: goal 0 with finishedCount 0 gives NaN (Math.min(100, NaN) is NaN, hence strokeDasharray='NaN, 100'), and with any finished book gives Infinity, which Math.min clamps harmlessly to 100 — so the NaN render needs both conditions. One correction to the stated reachability: the backup import cannot supply this value, since importLibrary (useLibrary.tsx:102-122) merges only books and summaries and never touches the profile. The real ingress is migrate.ts:93 `monthlyGoal: legacyProfile?.monthlyGoal` taken off the JSON.parse assertion, because repo.ts:21's `?? 4` rescues null and undefined but not 0 (and not a string). Low stands: an invalid SVG attribute and a mis-drawn ring.
findings.reachability: Legacy localStorage profile with `monthlyGoal: 0` -> migrate.ts:93 -> repo.ts:21 keeps the 0 -> ProfileView renders strokeDasharray='NaN, 100' until the user drags the goal slider. The range input itself (min='1', line 235) cannot produce 0.
findings.blastRadius: 1 divide (ProfileView.tsx:53), 1 render (line 209), 1 writer (line 239) plus the migration ingress at migrate.ts:93.
findings.suggestedPatch: Sanitise at the repo so the bad value never persists — repo.ts:21: `monthlyGoal: Number.isInteger(input.monthlyGoal) && (input.monthlyGoal as number) > 0 ? (input.monthlyGoal as number) : 4;` — and guard the divide at ProfileView.tsx:53: `profile.monthlyGoal > 0 ? Math.min(100, (finishedCount / profile.monthlyGoal) * 100) : 0`. Risk: none; both are defaults that only fire on values the UI cannot produce.

findings.title: `e.target?.result as string` erases three real possibilities from FileReader's result
findings.description: `ProgressEvent.target` is `EventTarget | null` and `FileReader.result` is `string | ArrayBuffer | null`, so the expression's honest type is `string | ArrayBuffer | null | undefined`. The `as string` tells the compiler all four cases are one. On the happy path `readAsText` does produce a string, but on an aborted or failed read `result` is `null`, and `JSON.parse(null)` coerces to the string `'null'` and returns `null` - so `data` is `null`, line 119's `data.books` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`, and the user gets the generic 'Could not read that backup file.' message with no indication the read itself failed. The assertion is currently masked by the surrounding catch rather than being correct, and it is the same cast that feeds the unvalidated write in L11-F04. FIX SHAPE: narrow instead of assert - `const result = e.target?.result; if (typeof result !== 'string') { toast.error(...); return; }` - which costs two lines and removes both the lie and the misleading error message.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present, but the stated failure scenario is factually wrong and the assertion holds at runtime — amending medium -> low. Verified verbatim at src/components/ProfileView.tsx:113-117: `const reader = new FileReader(); reader.onload = async (e) => { try { const content = e.target?.result as string;`, with `reader.readAsText(file)` at line 142. The typing analysis is correct as far as it goes — `ProgressEvent.target` is `EventTarget | null` and `FileReader.result` is `string | ArrayBuffer | null`, so the honest type is `string | ArrayBuffer | null | undefined` and `as string` collapses four possibilities into one. THE FAILURE SCENARIO DOES NOT HOLD: the finding says 'on an aborted or failed read `result` is null', but `FileReader` fires `load` only on successful termination — a failed read fires `error` and an abort fires `abort`, and neither routes to `reader.onload`. Inside this handler `e.target` is always the FileReader and `result` is always the `readAsText` string. So `JSON.parse(null)` is never actually invoked here. (I did confirm the mechanic in isolation under node — `JSON.parse(null)` coerces to `'null'` and returns `null`, which would make line 119's `data.books` throw — but that path is unreachable from `onload`.) The assertion is therefore runtime-correct, which the spec's verification criterion 2 says is a lower-severity outcome: 'A perfect match with the cast still loses (could've been a real type), but lower-severity.' The genuinely damaging cast in this handler is the NEXT line — `const data = JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport;` at ProfileView.tsx:117, which is already filed and confirmed at `high` as F051. Standalone, line 116 is a lie with no victim, so `low` is the honest calibration. The fix is still worth the two lines because it removes the lie and, when combined with the F051 guard, produces a truthful error message instead of the generic 'Could not read that backup file.'
findings.reachability: The assertion never misfires on a reachable path. Profile -> Data Management -> Import Data (ProfileView.tsx:327-333) -> `handleImport` (line 109) -> `reader.readAsText(file)` (line 142); `onload` runs only on success, where `result` is a string. Read failures and aborts bypass this handler entirely — and note there is no `reader.onerror` handler at all here, so a failed read currently produces silence rather than a wrong value.
findings.blastRadius: One `onload` handler in one component. `content` feeds exactly one expression, `JSON.parse(content)` at line 117. No test file exists for ProfileView (src/components/ contains zero *.test.tsx).
findings.amendedDescription: `e.target?.result as string` at src/components/ProfileView.tsx:116 collapses the honest type `string | ArrayBuffer | null | undefined` (from `ProgressEvent.target: EventTarget | null` and `FileReader.result: string | ArrayBuffer | null`) into `string` by assertion. The typing critique is correct, but the reported failure is not reachable: `FileReader` fires `load` only on successful termination — failures fire `error` and aborts fire `abort`, neither of which routes to this handler — so inside `onload` after `readAsText` (line 142) `result` is always a string and the claimed `JSON.parse(null)` path never executes. (The mechanic itself is real in isolation: `JSON.parse(null)` returns `null`, which would make line 119's `data.books` throw.) Downgraded to `low` per the spec's rule that a cast whose runtime value matches is lower-severity. The damaging cast on this path is the adjacent `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` at line 117, already confirmed at `high` as F051; fix both together. Worth noting separately: there is no `reader.onerror` handler here at all, so a genuinely failed read produces silence.

findings.title: `Record<string, number>` claims total key coverage; only a `|| 0` coercion saves the read of a key that does not exist yet
findings.description: `Record<string, number>` asserts that *every* string key yields a `number`. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off, `categoryMap[b.category]` on line 25 is typed `number` while returning `undefined` on the first occurrence of each category — `undefined + 1` would be `NaN`, and the only thing preventing a row of "NaN book(s)" in the Category Breakdown is the `|| 0` fallback. The code is correct today; the *type* is not, and the correctness depends on a coercion the compiler cannot see. This is the clearest small illustration of what enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would buy: it would type this access `number | undefined` and force the fallback to be visible in the type, and it would simultaneously flag the genuinely dangerous accesses (L12-F04's `options[correctAnswerIndex]`, L12-F13's `items[0]!`). Cost is not a switch flip — every array index and `Record` read in the repo would need review — but the repo is small and already clean under `strict: true`, so it is achievable. Fix shape: either `Map<string, number>` (whose `get` honestly returns `| undefined`) or enable the flag.
findings.verifierNote: Verified: StatsView.tsx:23 `const categoryMap: Record<string, number> = {};` and line 25 `categoryMap[b.category] = (categoryMap[b.category] || 0) + 1;`. The Record type does assert total key coverage, so with noUncheckedIndexedAccess off the read on line 25 is typed `number` while returning undefined on the first occurrence of each category; only the `|| 0` coercion prevents `undefined + 1` from producing NaN and a 'NaN book(s)' row in the Category Breakdown at StatsView.tsx:133-138. Correct today, type wrong today — exactly the low tier. The identical shape exists at ProfileView.tsx:59-61 (categoryCounts), so the pattern is duplicated rather than isolated. The finding is honest that this is an illustration of F109's flag, not an independent bug.
findings.reachability: Runs on every StatsView render; the undefined is real on the first book of each category and is absorbed by `|| 0`.
findings.blastRadius: 2 sites of the same shape (StatsView.tsx:23-26, ProfileView.tsx:59-62).
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the miss honest without waiting on the flag: `const categoryMap = new Map<string, number>(); books.forEach((b) => categoryMap.set(b.category, (categoryMap.get(b.category) ?? 0) + 1));` and `const categoryData = [...categoryMap.entries()].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);` at line 28. Risk: line 28's Object.entries call must change with it; same edit applies at ProfileView.tsx:59-67.

findings.title: Pending-confirm state is split across a nullable state field and a nullable ref that the types never tie together, so `Promise<boolean>` can hang forever
findings.description: A pending confirmation is one logical thing represented as two independent nullable slots: `options: ConfirmOptions | null` (line 18) and `resolverRef: ((value: boolean) => void) | null` (line 19). The invariant `options !== null` <=> `resolverRef.current !== null` is real but unencoded, and the code violates it: `confirm()` assigns `resolverRef.current = resolve` unconditionally (line 24), so a second `confirm()` issued while one is pending overwrites the first resolver with no trace. The first promise then never settles. The declared contract `type ConfirmFn = (options: ConfirmOptions) => Promise<boolean>` (line 13) claims every call yields a settling promise; the runtime does not deliver that. Concrete failure: a consumer does `if (!(await confirm({...}))) return;` before a destructive action (all three consumers do — ProfilePage.tsx:10, BookDetailPage.tsx:16, ProfileView.tsx:49). If a second confirm is raised — a double-click on a delete control, or a second component racing on the same provider — the first `await` never resumes, so its `finally`/spinner-reset never runs and its enclosing async function is retained forever. The same shape means unmounting the provider mid-confirm leaks a pending promise. The `?? ''` and `?.` fallbacks scattered through the JSX (lines 41, 45, 51, 56, 61) exist purely because the type cannot express "open implies options". Fix shape: one state value shaped as a discriminated union — `{ status: 'idle' } | { status: 'pending'; options: ConfirmOptions; resolve: (v: boolean) => void }` — and have `confirm()` settle any existing pending entry with `false` before replacing it. Blast radius: 3 consumers, all on destructive paths (delete profile, delete book).
findings.verifierNote: The code is exactly as described: ConfirmDialog.tsx:18-19 holds the pending confirm in two independent nullable slots and confirm() at :21-26 assigns `resolverRef.current = resolve` unconditionally, so a second pending confirm would strand the first promise. What does NOT hold is reachability. ConfirmProvider renders a single Dialog (:39-44) and Dialog.tsx:21-29 mounts a `fixed inset-0 z-50` backdrop only while open, whose onClick settles the pending confirm with false. All three consumers call confirm() as the first statement of a click/FileReader handler (ProfilePage.tsx:16, BookDetailPage.tsx:28, ProfileView.tsx:125), so React flushes the discrete-event update and mounts the backdrop before a second click can reach any trigger. I could not construct a path in the current app where two confirms are pending simultaneously. The provider-unmount leak is real but costs only a retained closure whose continuation is `if (!confirmed) return`. Amended down to low: genuine latent modelling defect, no current incident path.
findings.reachability: Not reachable today - the single full-screen modal makes confirmation exclusive by construction. Re-opens the moment anyone adds a non-blocking confirm surface (inline/toast-style), a second ConfirmProvider, or a programmatic confirm not driven by a user click.
findings.blastRadius: 3 non-test consumers (ProfileView.tsx:125 backup import, ProfilePage.tsx:16 delete-whole-library, BookDetailPage.tsx:28 delete-book).
findings.suggestedPatch: Collapse the two slots into one tagged state: `type Pending = { status: 'idle' } | { status: 'pending'; options: ConfirmOptions; resolve: (v: boolean) => void }`, and inside the Promise executor do `setPending((prev) => { if (prev.status === 'pending') prev.resolve(false); return { status: 'pending', options: next, resolve }; })`. Render the Dialog body only when pending, which deletes the five `?.`/`?? ''` fallbacks at :41/45/51/56/61. Risk: `resolve` must be captured inside `new Promise`, so the state update has to happen in the executor rather than before it.
findings.amendedDescription: ConfirmDialog holds one logical pending-confirm as two unrelated nullable slots (options state at :18, resolver ref at :19), and confirm() at :24 overwrites any in-flight resolver, so the invariant 'open implies options implies resolver' is unencoded and violable. No current call path can produce two pending confirms - the provider's single full-screen modal backdrop (Dialog.tsx:24-29) makes confirmation exclusive - so this is latent refactor risk, not a live hang. Fixing it also removes the five `?.`/`?? ''` fallbacks the current shape forces in the JSX.

findings.title: `Dialog`'s `size` prop is a bare `string` where only a handful of Tailwind max-width classes are valid
findings.description: `size?: string` accepts any string, but the only values that do anything are Tailwind max-width utilities — and Tailwind's JIT compiler only emits classes it finds in the source, so a typo (`max-w-mdd`), a runtime-computed value, or a plausible-looking alternative (`w-96`) compiles cleanly, passes lint, and produces a dialog with no width constraint at all: the panel stretches to the full flex container. Nothing fails; the layout is just silently wrong, and only on the one screen that used the bad value. The existing call sites pass `"max-w-md"` (ConfirmDialog.tsx:42) and `"max-w-lg"` (ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38) with the `"max-w-xl"` default (line 15), so a three-member literal union — or a `'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'` token mapped to classes inside Dialog — would cover every use and make the invalid states unrepresentable. Fix shape: replace `string` with a literal union; trivial effort, 3 call sites.
findings.verifierNote: Verified. Dialog.tsx:11-12 declares `/** Tailwind max-width class for the panel. */ size?: string`, line 15 defaults it to 'max-w-xl', and line 35 interpolates it directly into the panel className. The failure mode described is accurate for a JIT-compiled Tailwind setup (@tailwindcss/vite, vite.config.ts:3): a class the compiler never sees in source is simply not emitted, so a typo yields a panel with no width constraint that stretches to the flex container at Dialog.tsx:24 — no error, no test failure, wrong layout on one screen only. Call sites re-counted: exactly two pass a value (ConfirmDialog.tsx:43 'max-w-md', ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38 'max-w-lg') and one relies on the default (AddBookModal.tsx:100), so a three-member union covers every existing use with no call-site churn. Low and trivial, as claimed.
findings.reachability: Any future caller passing a mistyped or non-emitted class. No current call site is wrong.
findings.blastRadius: 3 call sites (2 explicit, 1 default) against 1 prop declaration.
findings.suggestedPatch: Dialog.tsx:12 -> `size?: 'max-w-md' | 'max-w-lg' | 'max-w-xl';`. Both existing values are members, so no call site changes. Risk: a future width needs the union extended — which is the intent; keep the JSDoc note that Tailwind must see the literal in source to emit the class.

findings.title: Redundant non-null assertions on array indices mark a tsconfig gap the tests would then mask
findings.description: `const [a, b] = getToasts(); expect(a!.id).not.toBe(b!.id)` (lines 24-25) and `dismissToast(getToasts()[0]!.id)` (line 30) apply `!` to values the compiler already types as non-optional: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off, so `getToasts()[0]` and a destructured element both infer as ToastMessage. The assertions are therefore no-ops that the type system does not need -- they signal the authors expected the flag to be on. The finding is forward-looking: these `!`s are pre-installed suppressions. If noUncheckedIndexedAccess is ever enabled (a change that would correctly surface the real lying-index type at useReviewQueue.ts:46, see L14-F07), this file and the same pattern at reviewQueue.test.tsx:95/112 will keep compiling silently instead of flagging that the tests assume a non-empty array. Fix shape: drop the redundant `!` now, or assert length first, so that enabling the flag produces an honest signal. Separately, the suite covers only the 'error' and 'success' arms of ToastKind; the 'info' arm is safe only because Toast.tsx:8 uses `Record<ToastKind, ...>`, which the compiler checks exhaustively.
findings.verifierNote: Verified verbatim: toastStore.test.ts:24-25 `const [a, b] = getToasts(); expect(a!.id).not.toBe(b!.id);` and line 30 `dismissToast(getToasts()[0]!.id);`. With noUncheckedIndexedAccess off (tsconfig.json:8 confirmed), both a destructured element and `getToasts()[0]` already infer as ToastMessage, so the `!` are no-ops the type system does not need — the reading that the authors pre-installed suppressions for a flag that is not on is well supported. The companion sites are also real: reviewQueue.test.tsx:95 and :112 both do `Date.parse(stored!.dueAt)` while the adjacent assertions on the same value use `stored?.id` and `stored?.intervalDays`, so the file mixes both idioms line by line. The forward-looking argument holds: enabling the flag (F109) would leave these files compiling silently instead of surfacing the non-empty-array assumption. Low is right — no runtime effect today.
findings.reachability: No runtime effect; the assertions are erased at compile time. The cost is future: the `!`s pre-suppress the diagnostic that enabling noUncheckedIndexedAccess is meant to produce.
findings.blastRadius: 4 redundant assertions across 2 test files (toastStore.test.ts 25, 30; reviewQueue.test.tsx 95, 112).
findings.suggestedPatch: Assert the precondition instead of suppressing it: `expect(getToasts()).toHaveLength(2); const [a, b] = getToasts(); expect(a?.id).not.toBe(b?.id);` at lines 24-25, and drop the `!` at line 30 (it compiles today) — same treatment at reviewQueue.test.tsx:95/112. Risk: none now; once the flag is enabled the un-asserted forms fail to compile, which is the intended signal.

findings.title: `document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null` asserts a `.focus()` method onto a base `Element`
findings.description: `document.activeElement` is `Element | null`. `Element` has no `focus()` — the cast is what makes `restoreTo?.focus()` on line 29 compile, and the `?.` guards only nullness, not the method's existence. In practice most focusable nodes are `HTMLElement` or `SVGElement` (both of which implement `focus()`), so this is Low rather than a live crash; the concrete risk is that the assertion is the only thing standing between the cleanup path and a `restoreTo.focus is not a function` TypeError thrown from an effect teardown — i.e. during unmount, where React surfaces it as an app-level error rather than a dismissible one. Fix shape: narrow with `instanceof HTMLElement` (or feature-test `'focus' in el`) instead of asserting; that also documents the intent. Same blast radius as L12-F07 (every modal in the app).
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present verbatim at useFocusTrap.ts:25 - `const restoreTo = document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null;`. `document.activeElement` is typed `Element | null` in lib.dom.d.ts and `Element` declares no `focus()`; the assertion is the only reason `restoreTo?.focus()` at :29 compiles, and `?.` guards nullness, not method existence. Severity `low` is right and honestly argued: every realistic `activeElement` (including `document.body`) is an `HTMLElement` or `SVGElement`, both of which do declare `focus()`, so no crash is reachable today. It is a genuine `as T` over a base type where a narrow is available, which is exactly the category. Not generated code; the file is hand-written and carries a doc comment (:7-12).
findings.reachability: Cleanup path of the effect at :22-31, which runs on every modal close (Dialog, ConfirmDialog, chat drawer, quiz). Reached constantly; the assertion just never turns out to be wrong.
findings.blastRadius: 1 assertion, 1 file; behaviourally it governs focus restore for every modal in the app.
findings.suggestedPatch: useFocusTrap.ts:25 -> `const restoreTo = document.activeElement;` (drop the cast) and :29 -> `if (restoreTo instanceof HTMLElement || restoreTo instanceof SVGElement) restoreTo.focus();`. Risk: `instanceof` is false across realms, so an element focused in another document would no longer be restored - not a case this app can produce.

findings.title: Optional chain over Array.find's Book | undefined makes the summaryId assertion vacuous
findings.description: `imported.find(...)` (line 53) returns `Book | undefined`, and the test then narrows with `?.` rather than proving the book exists. Line 55, `expect(atomic?.summaryId).toBeUndefined()`, PASSES when `atomic` itself is undefined -- i.e. if the Atomic Habits row were never imported at all, the assertion that it has no summary would still be green. This is the mirror-image of a non-null assertion: instead of lying that a value exists, the optional chain silently converts a type-level `| undefined` into a passing test. The only reason the suite still catches a missing book is the incidental `toHaveLength(2)` at line 51 and the fact that lines 56 and 60 use matchers that throw on undefined. Fix shape: `expect(atomic).toBeDefined()` first, then assert on a narrowed value, so the 'row not imported' failure mode reports as a failure rather than as a pass. Same optional-chain-over-index pattern in reviewQueue.test.tsx:93-96 and 110-111, where `const [stored] = ...` is then mixed inconsistently as `stored?.id` and `stored!.dueAt` on adjacent lines.
findings.verifierNote: The optional chain exists at goodreadsImport.test.tsx:55 (`expect(atomic?.summaryId).toBeUndefined()`), but the stated failure mode is wrong. Line 54 - one line ABOVE the cited line - is `expect(atomic).toMatchObject({ status: 'Finished', rating: 5, readingTimeMinutes: 0 })`, and toMatchObject throws on an undefined received value. The 'Atomic Habits row was never imported' case therefore fails loudly at :54 and :55 is never reached with `atomic === undefined`. The discovery reasoning enumerates :51, :56 and :60 as the incidental safety net and simply omits :54, which is a direct, non-incidental assertion on `atomic` itself. Same for the reviewQueue.test.tsx half: :95 and :112 use `stored!.dueAt`, which throws a TypeError and fails the test if `stored` is undefined - loud, not silent. What remains is cosmetic: `?.` in assertions on values already proven defined, and `?.`/`!` mixed on adjacent lines. Amended to low (hygiene).
findings.reachability: No silent-pass path exists. The only way to reach :55 is with `atomic` already proven non-undefined by :54.
findings.blastRadius: 2 test files, 6 assertion lines (goodreadsImport.test.tsx:55-56, reviewQueue.test.tsx:94-96 and :111-112). Zero production code.
findings.suggestedPatch: goodreadsImport.test.tsx: fold summaryId/coverImageUrl into the existing :54 toMatchObject, or `expect(atomic).toBeDefined();` then assert on `atomic!`. reviewQueue.test.tsx:93 / :110 -> `const stored = (await reviewCards.listByProfile(profile.id))[0]!;` then plain member access on :94-96 and :111-112. Risk: none - test-only, behaviour-preserving.
findings.amendedDescription: goodreadsImport.test.tsx:55-56 assert through `?.` on an `Array.find` result. The claimed 'passes when atomic is undefined' hole does not exist: line 54's `expect(atomic).toMatchObject(...)` already fails on an undefined receiver, so a missing row is reported as a failure before line 55 runs. The residual issue is stylistic - optional chains implying a nullability the surrounding test has already excluded, plus `?.` mixed with `!` on adjacent lines in reviewQueue.test.tsx:94-95 and 111-112.

findings.title: Import workflow held as three independent states, letting a failed pick import the previous file's rows
findings.description: `preview`, `filename` and `isImporting` model one linear workflow as three orthogonal states -- eight representable combinations for four legal ones (`filename` set with `preview` null, and vice versa, are both representable and both meaningless). The illegal combination is reachable: `handleFile`'s catch on line 30 toasts and returns without clearing `preview` or `filename`, because both are only assigned on the success path (lines 25-26). Concrete failure: the user picks A.csv successfully (preview shows '100 books found', the drop zone shows 'A.csv'), then re-opens the picker and chooses B.csv, whose read rejects -- `file.text()` throws `DOMException: NotReadableError` / `NotFoundError` when the file was moved, deleted, or its permission revoked between selection and read, and on a disconnected network share. The user sees 'Could not read that file.' but the drop zone still reads 'A.csv', the preview still reads '100 books found', and the Import button is still enabled; clicking it imports A's rows while the user believes they are importing B. Correct shape: a single tagged state, `{ phase: 'idle' } | { phase: 'parsed'; filename: string; result: GoodreadsParseResult } | { phase: 'importing'; ... }`, which makes the stale combination unrepresentable and forces the error path to transition explicitly. Blast radius: this component only, but the outcome is persisted book records.
findings.verifierNote: Code confirmed line-for-line: GoodreadsImport.tsx:15-17 holds three orthogonal states, :25-26 assigns preview and filename only on the success path, and the catch at :30-32 toasts without clearing either, so the illegal combination is reachable and the Import button at :98 (`disabled={!preview || preview.rows.length === 0 || isImporting}`) stays enabled against the previous file's rows. Two things narrow it. (1) The only trigger is a throw from `await file.text()` at :24 - a zero-row or malformed CSV does NOT throw (parseGoodreadsCsv returns `{rows: [], skipped}` for a short table, goodreads.ts:78-80), and in that case :25-26 correctly overwrite the preview and :98 disables the button. So the failure needs a DOMException (file moved/deleted/permission revoked/disconnected share between pick and read). (2) The harm is bounded: the drop zone still shows the OLD filename at :75, visibly contradicting the error toast, and the rows imported are from a file the user did select, deduped by title|author at useLibrary.tsx:132-137. Amended to low: real impossible-state bug, rare trigger, low harm.
findings.reachability: Pick A.csv (success) -> pick B.csv whose read rejects -> toast 'Could not read that file.' while the drop zone still shows A.csv and '100 books found' -> clicking Import imports A's rows. Requires the file to become unreadable between selection and read.
findings.blastRadius: 1 component, 3 useState slots; the outcome is persisted book records, but only ones the user previously selected.
findings.suggestedPatch: Replace the three slots with `useState<{ phase: 'idle' } | { phase: 'parsed'; filename: string; result: GoodreadsParseResult } | { phase: 'importing'; filename: string; result: GoodreadsParseResult }>({ phase: 'idle' })` and make the catch at :30 call `setState({ phase: 'idle' })` before the toast. Risk: none beyond updating the four JSX reads at :75, :79-92 and :98.
findings.amendedDescription: GoodreadsImport models one linear workflow as three independent states (:15-17), making 'filename set, preview null' and its inverse representable. The catch at :30-32 reaches the illegal combination - it reports the error without clearing preview/filename, so the drop zone keeps showing the previous file and the still-enabled Import button (:98) will import the previous file's rows. Reachable only when `await file.text()` (:24) rejects (a parse failure or empty CSV does not, because :25-26 run first and :98 then disables the button), and bounded by the title|author dedupe in useLibrary.tsx:132-137.

findings.title: The 'All' sentinel shares a value space with real, AI-generated category strings
findings.description: `activeCategory` is a bare `string` whose sentinel value 'All' lives in the same value space as real `book.category` values, and `Book.category` is itself untyped (`category: string`, src/types.ts:33) and populated from unconstrained model output: src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:26 `category: data.category || 'Other'`, whose response schema declares only `{ type: Type.STRING }` (src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:8) -- the eight-value constraint exists solely as English in the prompt (src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:12), and the `Category` enum in types.ts:6 is never bound to the field. So the set is NOT closed by the buttons: `categories` on line 65 is derived from stored data. If the model ever returns 'All' for a book, `categories` contains 'All' twice, `key={cat}` on line 173 collides, and the second button -- which looks like a category filter -- short-circuits the check on line 47 and shows every book instead of that category's. The same collision silently makes `showRecommendations` (line 110) true when a real category is selected. The file already demonstrates the correct pattern one line below: `statusFilter` is typed `'All' | BookStatus` (line 23). Fix shape: type the sentinel out of the data space -- `null` for 'no filter', or a tagged `{ kind: 'all' } | { kind: 'category'; name: string }` -- and narrow `Book.category` to the `Category` enum. Blast radius: this page's filter row.
findings.verifierNote: All cited lines present and unchanged: LibraryPage.tsx:22 `useState<string>('All')`, :47 `activeCategory === 'All' || book.category === activeCategory`, :65 `const categories = ['All', ...Array.from(new Set(books.map((b) => b.category)))]`, :173 `key={cat}`, :110 `activeCategory === 'All'`. The sentinel genuinely shares a value space with data: `Book.category` is `string` (types.ts:33), the `Category` enum (types.ts:6-15) is never bound to it, and summarize.ts writes `data.category || 'Other'` from a `Type.STRING` schema, so the eight-value constraint is prompt English only. If a stored category is literally 'All' the derived array holds it twice, React keys collide at :173, and the second button silently shows the whole library. The file's own `statusFilter` at :23 (`useState<'All' | BookStatus>`) demonstrates the correct pattern one line down. Low is correct - it needs the model to emit exactly 'All'.
findings.reachability: Requires a persisted `Book.category === 'All'`. Producible only via the LLM path (summarize.ts:26) or a hand-edited record; Goodreads import hardcodes 'Other' (useLibrary.tsx:154). Not reachable on any deterministic path today.
findings.blastRadius: 1 page - the filter row, the `categories` derivation, and `showRecommendations` at :106-110. No exported type changes.
findings.suggestedPatch: `const [activeCategory, setActiveCategory] = useState<string | null>(null);` then :47 `activeCategory === null || book.category === activeCategory`, :110 `activeCategory === null`, :65 `const categories = Array.from(new Set(books.map((b) => b.category)));`, and render the All button outside the `.map` with `onClick={() => setActiveCategory(null)}` / `aria-pressed={activeCategory === null}`. Risk: the All button must move out of the map so its key stays distinct from data-derived keys.

findings.title: Priority score map typed `Record<string, number>` instead of `Record<Priority, number>`
findings.description: The key domain is `Priority` ('Low' | 'Medium' | 'High', src/types.ts:2), not `string`. Typing the map with a `string` index signature has two costs. First, the map stops being exhaustive: adding a fourth `Priority` value compiles cleanly and silently scores it 1, changing the 'Want to Read' ordering with no compile error anywhere. Second, the index access is a small lie in both directions -- with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (confirmed in tsconfig.json) `priorityScore[...]` is typed `number` and never `undefined`, so the `?? 1` fallbacks on lines 57-58 are unreachable as far as the compiler is concerned while reading as though they were load-bearing; they are in fact dead, because `a.priority || 'Low'` can only produce a key that exists. `Record<Priority, number>` makes the literal exhaustive, makes the lookup genuinely total, and lets both `?? 1` fallbacks be deleted. Blast radius: the sort comparator on this page.
findings.verifierNote: Present at LibraryPage.tsx:56 `const priorityScore: Record<string, number> = { High: 3, Medium: 2, Low: 1 };` with `?? 1` at :57-58. The key domain really is `Priority` ('Low' | 'Medium' | 'High', types.ts:2, used at types.ts:35 `priority?: Priority`). Both claims check out: (a) the `string` index signature makes the literal non-exhaustive, so a fourth `Priority` member would compile and silently score 1; (b) `a.priority || 'Low'` can only produce one of the three declared keys, and with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off the lookup is typed `number`, so both `?? 1` fallbacks are dead in both the type sense and the runtime sense while reading as though load-bearing. Category `weak-type-as-Object-or-Function` is a loose but acceptable fit (an over-wide index signature rather than a literal `Object`/`{}`); no better bucket exists in the spec's list.
findings.reachability: The comparator runs on every LibraryPage render whenever two 'Want to Read' books are compared - constantly. Nothing misbehaves today; the exposure is a future 4th Priority value.
findings.blastRadius: 1 sort comparator on 1 page; `Priority` has 3 usages repo-wide.
findings.suggestedPatch: `import type { Priority } from '../../types';` and `const priorityScore: Record<Priority, number> = { High: 3, Medium: 2, Low: 1 };`, then delete both `?? 1` at :57-58. Risk: none - `a.priority || 'Low'` is already `Priority`; a future 4th value becomes a compile error at the literal, which is the point.

findings.title: A recommendation title doubles as its identity for both the React key and the in-flight marker
findings.description: `addingBookTitle: string | null` is a raw title used as an identity: it is compared against `rec.title` on lines 109 and 149 to decide which card shows the 'Generating...' spinner, and `rec.title` is also the React reconciliation key on line 81. Nothing guarantees titles are unique -- `Recommendation[]` comes from `getAIRecommendations` (src/lib/ai/recommend.ts:34), which maps model output straight through with no dedupe, and the defaults in recommendationDefaults.ts are a separate list that a refreshed set can overlap. Concrete failure: the model returns two entries with the same title (a common case for reissues, or a title the model repeats), so the list renders duplicate React keys and, once the user clicks one, BOTH cards show the 'Generating...' spinner while only one summary is being fetched -- and clicking the other is silently swallowed by the `if (addingBookTitle) return;` guard at LibraryPage.tsx:87. A distinct identity on `Recommendation` (or an index-based key plus an index-based in-flight marker) removes the ambiguity; a branded `RecommendationId` would make the title/identity mixup a compile error. Blast radius: the carousel and LibraryPage's preview flow.
findings.evidence:
12    addingBookTitle: string | null;
...
81            key={rec.title}
...
109                  {addingBookTitle === rec.title ? (
110                    <>
111                      <Loader2 size={12} className="animate-spin" /> Generating...
...
149                    {addingBookTitle === rec.title ? (
findings.verifierNote: All cited lines confirmed: RecommendationCarousel.tsx:12 `addingBookTitle: string | null`, :81 `key={rec.title}`, :109 and :149 `addingBookTitle === rec.title`. The duplicate-title failure is real - `getAIRecommendations` (recommend.ts:33-38) maps model output through `(data.recommendations ?? []).map(...)` with no dedupe, and LibraryPage.tsx:87 `if (addingBookTitle) return;` swallows the second click. But the FIX SHAPE in the finding is wrong, which is why this is amended rather than confirmed: a branded `RecommendationId` would not confer uniqueness - branding prevents cross-domain substitution, not collisions - and the live defect is that `Recommendation` (recommend.ts:9-14) declares no identity field at all. The branded-type angle that does survive is the weaker one: the in-flight marker is a bare `string` compared against `rec.title`, so `setAddingBookTitle(rec.author)` would compile. Severity stays `low`.
findings.reachability: LibraryPage.tsx:88 sets the marker from `rec.title`; requires the model to return two entries with the same title in one response (reissues, series volumes) or an AI refresh that overlaps `RECOMMENDED_BOOKS`. Plausible, unproven.
findings.blastRadius: 2 files - RecommendationCarousel (1 key + 2 spinner comparisons) and LibraryPage's preview flow (:27, :87-88, :100, :225).
findings.suggestedPatch: Track position instead of text: in LibraryPage `const [addingIndex, setAddingIndex] = useState<number | null>(null)`, pass `addingIndex`, and in the carousel `recommendations.map((rec, index) => ...)` with `key={index}` and `addingIndex === index`. Risk: index stability requires `recommendations` not to be reordered mid-flight, which it is not (`setRecommendations` only runs in `refreshRecommendations`, blocked while a preview is in flight).
findings.amendedDescription: The carousel uses `rec.title` as both the React reconciliation key (:81) and the in-flight identity (`addingBookTitle === rec.title` at :109 and :149), but `Recommendation` (lib/ai/recommend.ts:9-14) declares no identity field and `getAIRecommendations` (:33-38) does not dedupe model output. Two same-titled entries therefore produce colliding React keys and light BOTH 'Generating...' spinners while only one summary is fetched - and the second click is swallowed by `if (addingBookTitle) return;` at LibraryPage.tsx:87. The fix is an explicit identity, not a brand: branding a string does not make it unique. The genuine (smaller) branded-type angle is that the in-flight marker is a bare `string`, so `setAddingBookTitle(rec.author)` would type-check.

findings.title: The 'no active profile' precondition is unrepresentable in the mutators' return types, and is reported to the user as success
findings.description: Three sibling mutators handle the same precondition three different ways, and two of them encode failure as a legitimate-looking result. `importGoodreadsRows` returns `{ added: 0, duplicates: 0 }` for 'no profile' -- byte-identical to 'the file parsed but every row was already in the library' -- and GoodreadsImport.tsx:39-43 renders that as a green `toast.success('Imported 0 books.')`. `importLibrary` (line 104) returns `0` for the same state, which ProfileView.tsx:133 reports as 'Imported 0 new books.' Meanwhile `addBook` (line 42) throws `new Error('No active profile')` for the identical precondition. Honest reachability: App.tsx:22 does not mount `LibraryProvider` until `profile` is non-null, so these branches are dead in the current app -- the finding is that the return types cannot express the precondition, so nothing catches a future change to where the provider mounts, or a direct call from a test or a new caller, and the failure mode when it lands is a silent success message over dropped data. Fix shape: either make the precondition a type-level invariant (take the profile as an argument, so a null profile cannot reach the call) or return a tagged result so 'no profile' is a distinct case callers must handle. Blast radius: two call sites today, both user-facing toasts.
findings.evidence:
128  const importGoodreadsRows = useCallback(
129    async (rows: GoodreadsRow[]): Promise<{ added: number; duplicates: number }> => {
130      if (!profile) return { added: 0, duplicates: 0 };
...
41    if (!profile) throw new Error('No active profile');   // addBook, same precondition
...
104      if (!profile) return 0;                             // importLibrary, third contract
findings.verifierNote: Three contracts for one precondition confirmed in the current file: useLibrary.tsx:42 `if (!profile) throw new Error('No active profile');` (addBook), :104 `if (!profile) return 0;` (importLibrary), :130 `if (!profile) return { added: 0, duplicates: 0 };` (importGoodreadsRows). The success-shaped failure is real at both consumers: GoodreadsImport.tsx renders `toast.success(`Imported ${added} book...`)` which reads 'Imported 0 books.', and ProfileView.tsx:133 renders `toast.success(`Imported ${added} new book...`)`. Reachability is correctly self-limited by the finding and I verified it independently: App.tsx:22 returns `<ProfilePicker />` when `!profile` and only mounts `<LibraryProvider>` at :32 with a non-null profile, so all three branches are dead in the shipped app. The type-level point stands - `Promise<number>` and `Promise<{added,duplicates}>` cannot express the precondition, so nothing would catch a move of the provider or a new caller.
findings.reachability: Dead in-app (App.tsx:10-32 gates on both `isLoading` and `profile`). Live only for a direct call from a test or a future caller that mounts LibraryProvider higher in the tree.
findings.blastRadius: 3 mutators, 2 user-facing consumers. `LibraryApi = ReturnType<typeof useLibraryState>` (:185), so a signature change propagates to all consumers automatically.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the precondition a type-level invariant instead of a runtime branch: `function useLibraryState(profile: Profile)` and `export function LibraryProvider({ profile, children }: { profile: Profile; children: ReactNode })`, passing `profile` from App.tsx:32 where it is already narrowed non-null; then delete the branches at :42, :104 and :130. Risk: keep the `useProfile()` call for `profileLoading` at :25; any test that renders `LibraryProvider` directly must now pass a profile.

findings.title: The probe binds to an inferred hook contract in which current: queue[0] is typed ReviewCard, not ReviewCard | undefined
findings.description: `let api: ReturnType<typeof useReviewQueue>` inherits whatever the hook infers, and useReviewQueue (useReviewQueue.ts:8) declares no return type. Its `current: queue[0]` (useReviewQueue.ts:46) therefore infers as `ReviewCard`, not `ReviewCard | undefined`, because noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off -- the hook's public contract states that a card always exists, which is false the moment the queue empties (which is the normal end of every session, and the state asserted at lines 65 and 91). The test itself proves the type is wrong: lines 56, 77 and 128 all write `api.current?.question` with an optional chain the compiler considers unnecessary. A consumer that trusts the declared type and writes `current.question` compiles and crashes on the empty queue; ReviewPage.tsx:52 happens to guard with `if (!current)` but nothing in the type system requires that and no test would catch a consumer that omits it. The same untyped-return pattern applies to useLibraryState (useLibrary.tsx:17, re-exported as LibraryApi at line 185) and useTheme (useTheme.ts:14). Fix shape: annotate the hook's return with an explicit interface declaring `current: ReviewCard | undefined`.
findings.verifierNote: The observation is accurate - reviewQueue.test.tsx:10 binds `let api: ReturnType<typeof useReviewQueue>`, and :56, :77, :122 and :128 all write `api.current?.question` with an optional chain the compiler considers unnecessary because `queue[0]` infers as `ReviewCard` (tsconfig.json sets only `strict: true`, no noUncheckedIndexedAccess - I read it directly). But this is the test-side mirror of F074, not an independent defect: there is exactly one root cause (useReviewQueue.ts:8 has no return annotation) and one fix, and annotating the hook makes every `?.` in this test correct rather than redundant. Amended down to low and should be folded into F074 in the report rather than fixed separately. The extra detail worth keeping is that the test file is the evidence FOR F074: the author instinctively wrote `?.` against a type that claims it is unnecessary.
findings.reachability: No independent path. The test file cannot crash on this; it is the symptom that documents F074's inaccurate contract.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test file, 4 lines. Subsumed by F074's single-line fix.
findings.suggestedPatch: No separate change. After F074's fix (`current: ReviewCard | undefined`), leave reviewQueue.test.tsx:56/77/122/128 exactly as they are - the `?.` becomes required. Risk: none.
findings.amendedDescription: Test-side mirror of F074. reviewQueue.test.tsx:10 inherits the hook's inferred contract, in which `current: queue[0]` is typed `ReviewCard` rather than `ReviewCard | undefined`; the file's own `api.current?.question` at :56, :77, :122 and :128 is the evidence that the declared type is wrong. Fold into F074 - annotating the hook's return resolves this file with no edit.

findings.title: The theme union is re-declared inline instead of importing ThemeChoice
findings.description: renderWithTheme's parameter re-states the literal union `'system' | 'light' | 'dark'` rather than importing ThemeChoice (useTheme.ts:5), which is itself `Profile['theme']` (types.ts:23). Three copies of the same union now exist. If a fourth theme is added to Profile, this helper keeps compiling (the narrower literal union is still assignable to what profiles.create accepts, repo.ts:16), the new value is silently untested, and nothing flags the divergence. The same duplication pattern would apply to any future test helper that re-types a domain union. Fix shape: `import type { ThemeChoice } from './useTheme'` and annotate the parameter with it, so adding a theme forces the helper (and any exhaustive switch on it) to be revisited.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present at useTheme.test.tsx:15 `async function renderWithTheme(theme: 'system' | 'light' | 'dark')`. But the count is wrong: there are TWO literal spellings of the union, not three - types.ts:23 (`theme: 'system' | 'light' | 'dark'`, the canonical declaration) and this test helper. useTheme.ts:5 is `export type ThemeChoice = Profile['theme']`, a derivation that tracks the source automatically, not a copy. The consequence is also softer than stated: adding a 4th theme to `Profile` would leave this helper compiling and the new value untested, which is a test-coverage gap rather than a soundness one, and it is confined to a test file. `generic-opportunity` is a loose fit (there is no generic to extract - the fix is one import), but no better bucket exists in the spec's list. Keeping `low`; worth doing because it costs one line.
findings.reachability: Test-only. No production value flows through this annotation.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test helper, 6 call sites inside the same file (:51, :57, :63, :69, :74 and the inline render at :88).
findings.suggestedPatch: Add `import type { ThemeChoice } from './useTheme';` and change :15 to `async function renderWithTheme(theme: ThemeChoice)`. Risk: none - `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` requires the `import type` form, which this file already uses.
findings.amendedDescription: The theme union is spelled out literally in useTheme.test.tsx:15 instead of importing `ThemeChoice`. This is the second of two literal spellings (the other is the canonical declaration at types.ts:23); useTheme.ts:5 `export type ThemeChoice = Profile['theme']` is a derivation, not a third copy. Impact is test-scoped: adding a fourth theme to `Profile` leaves this helper compiling and the new value silently untested.

findings.title: vi.stubGlobal erases the matchMedia type, and the hand-built stub never fires a change event
findings.description: mockPrefersDark installs a hand-built matchMedia through vi.stubGlobal, whose value parameter is typed `unknown` -- TypeScript performs NO check that the stub satisfies `(query: string) => MediaQueryList`. The stub's `addEventListener: vi.fn()` records calls and never invokes the handler, so useTheme.ts:22-24 -- `const onChange = (event: MediaQueryListEvent) => setSystemDark(event.matches)` and the removeEventListener cleanup -- is dead code from this suite's point of view. Both 'system' tests (lines 61-71) set the preference BEFORE mount and assert the initial resolution from useState(systemPrefersDark) (useTheme.ts:17); nothing ever flips the preference while mounted. Compounding it, useTheme.ts:23-24 uses an optional call (`query.addEventListener?.(...)`), so if the stub -- or a real browser -- ever lacks that method the hook silently stops subscribing and every test still passes green. UNTESTED PRODUCTION BEHAVIOUR: a user on `theme: 'system'` who switches their OS between light and dark with the app open; the app should re-theme live and there is no test that it does.
findings.verifierNote: The facts check out: useTheme.test.tsx:27-39 installs a hand-built matchMedia via `vi.stubGlobal`, whose value parameter is `unknown`, so nothing checks the stub against `MediaQueryList`; `addEventListener: vi.fn()` (:32) records calls and never invokes the handler, so useTheme.ts:22-24 (`onChange` and the removeEventListener cleanup) is never exercised; both system tests (:61-71) set the preference before mount and assert the initial resolution from `useState(systemPrefersDark)` at useTheme.ts:17; and useTheme.ts:23-24's optional call (`query.addEventListener?.(...)`) means a stub - or a browser - lacking the method silently stops subscribing with every test still green. But the severity and the category are both off. The `unknown` belongs to Vitest's own stubGlobal signature, not to this codebase, and is genuinely correct for an API that can stub anything - the spec's own guidance is to accept type looseness at platform/library shims rather than file it. The stub is not a lying fixture either: it has every MediaQueryList member, just inert. What is left is a test-coverage gap whose worst outcome is that a live OS theme switch stops re-theming until reload - cosmetic. Amended to low.
findings.reachability: No production defect demonstrated. The untested behaviour is: user on `theme: 'system'` flips their OS appearance with the app open and the page does not re-theme until reload.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test helper (:26-40) and 1 unexercised effect (useTheme.ts:19-25). 1 non-test consumer of useTheme (AppShell).
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the stub type-checked and drivable: keep a module-scope `let changeHandler: ((e: MediaQueryListEvent) => void) | undefined;`, have the mock's `addEventListener: (_: string, fn: (e: MediaQueryListEvent) => void) => { changeHandler = fn; }`, annotate the factory `vi.fn((query: string): MediaQueryList => ({...}) as MediaQueryList)` so drift from the real interface is caught, then add one test that mounts with 'system', calls `act(() => changeHandler?.({ matches: true } as MediaQueryListEvent))` and asserts the `dark` class appears. Risk: none - test-only.
findings.amendedDescription: useTheme.test.tsx:27-39 installs a hand-built matchMedia through `vi.stubGlobal`, which accepts `unknown`, so the stub is never checked against `MediaQueryList` and could drift silently. Its `addEventListener` (:32) never invokes the handler, so useTheme.ts:22-24 - the live system-theme subscription and its cleanup - is dead code from this suite's point of view, and useTheme.ts:23's optional call means a missing method would go unnoticed in production too. Both 'system' tests (:61-71) only assert the initial resolution from useTheme.ts:17. Hygiene plus a coverage gap: the `unknown` is Vitest's API rather than a codebase choice, and the worst outcome is that a live OS theme switch fails to re-theme until reload.

findings.title: An unvalidated Profile.theme from IndexedDB is annotated into a three-literal union it may not belong to
findings.description:
`const theme: ThemeChoice = profile?.theme ?? 'system'` is the point where an unvalidated persisted value acquires a narrow type. `Profile` records come from `repo.profiles.list()`, which re-types raw IndexedDB rows without any runtime check, so `profile.theme` is `unknown` in practice. The `??` handles only null/undefined; a value like `"Dark"`, `"sepia"` or `"null"` passes straight through, and the explicit `ThemeChoice` annotation certifies to the compiler that it is one of `'system' | 'light' | 'dark'`. Line 27 then inherits the lie: the ternary's else-branch is believed to be `'light' | 'dark'` and is annotated `ResolvedTheme`, so `resolved` is typed as a two-literal union while holding an arbitrary string.

Concrete outcome (silent, not a crash): `classList.toggle('dark', resolved === 'dark')` at line 30 evaluates false, so the app renders in light mode with no error and no way for the user to tell why. In `ThemeToggle.tsx:24-26` the `theme === value` comparison is false for all three buttons, so `aria-pressed` is false on every one — the control group shows nothing selected, and a screen-reader user gets no current-state announcement. Clicking any button repairs it, so it self-heals on interaction.

Honest severity note: I traced every in-app writer and none can produce an out-of-union value. `repo.profiles.create` defaults `theme: input.theme ?? 'system'` (repo.ts:23); `useTheme.setTheme` only writes a `ThemeChoice`; `migrate.ts`'s `LegacyProfile` has no `theme` field at all, so migrated profiles get the default. The realistic vectors are a hand-edited IndexedDB record, a shared/downgraded browser profile, or a future theme value ('sepia' is a plausible addition given EReader owns its own reader themes) written by a newer build and read by an older one. Hence Low. The fix is a small parse-at-the-boundary guard rather than an annotation. Blast radius: `useTheme` is called at the shell level (`AppShell.tsx:31`) so it governs the whole app's dark mode.
findings.verifierNote: The line is present (useTheme.ts:16 `const theme: ThemeChoice = profile?.theme ?? 'system';`) and the downstream consequences described are accurate (:27 `resolved: ResolvedTheme`, :30 `classList.toggle('dark', resolved === 'dark')`, all-false `aria-pressed` in ThemeToggle). But the MECHANISM is misattributed, which is why this is amended: line 16 does not narrow anything. `profile` is `Profile | null` and `Profile['theme']` is already the three-literal union (types.ts:23), so the `: ThemeChoice` annotation is redundant - it restates a type the value already carries. The actual un-validated ingress is repo.ts:7-14, where `getAll('profiles')` / `get('profiles', id)` are typed purely by the `DBSchema` declaration in db.ts - already filed as F046 (high) and F094 (medium). So F133 is the highest-impact CONSUMER of that ingress, not an independent boundary. I re-verified the finding's own honest note: no in-app writer can produce an out-of-union theme (repo.ts:23 defaults `input.theme ?? 'system'`, useTheme.setTheme at :33-39 only writes a `ThemeChoice`, and migrate.ts's LegacyProfile has no theme field). Keeping `low`.
findings.reachability: Requires a persisted profile row with a non-union `theme` - hand-edited IndexedDB, a downgraded build, or a future 'sepia'. Not producible by any current code path. When it happens the app silently renders light with every ThemeToggle button un-pressed; self-heals on click.
findings.blastRadius: `useTheme()` is called at AppShell.tsx:31 so it governs app-wide dark mode; but the type weakness itself lives upstream at repo.ts:7-14 / db.ts (F046, F094), which serve every store, not just profiles.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add a small guard and use it instead of the annotation: `const THEMES = ['system', 'light', 'dark'] as const;` / `const asThemeChoice = (v: unknown): ThemeChoice => THEMES.includes(v as ThemeChoice) ? (v as ThemeChoice) : 'system';` then `const theme = asThemeChoice(profile?.theme);`. Risk: the guard holds the only cast, which is the intended shape; applying the same guard inside `repo.profiles.list/get` instead fixes every consumer at once but touches the shared read path.
findings.amendedDescription: Consumer-side mirror of the un-validated IndexedDB ingress already filed as F046 (repo.ts:8) and F094 (db.ts:9). useTheme.ts:16's `: ThemeChoice` annotation is redundant rather than causal - `profile.theme` already carries that type from types.ts:23 - so the lie is inherited, not created here. It is worth recording separately only because this is where the inherited lie has the widest blast radius: an out-of-union stored value silently renders light mode (:30) and leaves every ThemeToggle button `aria-pressed=false`, with no error and no way for the user to tell why. The correct fix is a parse-at-the-boundary guard (ideally inside `repo.profiles`, which also closes F046 for this field), not a change to the annotation.

findings.title: StatsPage destructures books without isLoading, so an unloaded library is typed identically to an empty one
findings.description:
`useLibrary()` returns `books: Book[]` alongside a separate `isLoading: boolean`, and `StatsPage` takes only `books`. `Book[]` cannot express 'not loaded yet', so the empty array returned before `reload()` resolves is indistinguishable — to the compiler and to the component — from a genuinely empty library. The type offers no prompt to check `isLoading`, and unlike `BookDetailPage.tsx:19` and `ReaderPage.tsx:14` (which do gate on `isLoading`), this page does not.

Concrete outcome: on navigation to /stats the user briefly sees a fully-rendered, confidently-wrong dashboard — 'Finished 0 out of 0', 'Total Learning 0m', 'Avg. Rating 0', 'No category data available yet', and the Wisdom Milestone copy reading 'enough knowledge to discuss deep concepts for over 0 hours straight' — which then flips to real numbers once IndexedDB responds. It reads as data loss for the instant it is on screen.

Verified negatives worth recording, because they were plausible and are not true: `StatsView` is arithmetic-safe on an empty array. Both `reduce` calls pass an initial value of 0 (StatsView.tsx:17, 20) so neither throws `TypeError` on an empty array; `avgRating` is guarded by `finished.length > 0` (line 19) so there is no NaN; and the only division by `stats.total` (line 153) sits inside a map over `categoryData`, which is empty whenever `total` is 0, so it never evaluates. No NaN and no throw — the defect is purely the untagged loading state.

Correct behavior: gate on `isLoading` here as the book pages do, or model the library state as a tagged union so the compiler forces the distinction. Blast radius: this page only; the underlying untagged loading bag in `useLibrary` is the shared root cause.
findings.verifierNote: StatsPage.tsx is 10 lines and reads exactly as cited: `const { books } = useLibrary();` at :6 with no `isLoading`, rendering `<StatsView books={books} .../>` at :9. The contrast is verified: BookDetailPage.tsx:19 `if (isLoading || !book || !profile)` and ReaderPage.tsx:14 both gate, as does ReviewPage.tsx:44 - StatsPage is the only route page that does not. `useLibrary` seeds `books` with `[]` (useLibrary.tsx:19) and only clears `isLoading` after the IndexedDB read (:32-33), so an unloaded library is literally `[]` and indistinguishable from an empty one. This is the concrete consumer instance of F023 (useLibrary.tsx:170, high, the untagged `{ books, isLoading }` bag); it stays a separate finding because the local fix is different from and far cheaper than F023's. The finding's verified negatives also hold - StatsView's reduces pass initial values, so no NaN and no throw.
findings.reachability: Every navigation to /stats: a fully rendered, confidently-wrong dashboard ('Finished 0 out of 0', 'Avg. Rating 0') for one IndexedDB round-trip, then it flips to real numbers.
findings.blastRadius: 1 page. The underlying untagged bag (F023) is consumed by every page that calls `useLibrary`.
findings.suggestedPatch:
`const { books, isLoading } = useLibrary();` plus the same guard the book pages use before :9 - e.g. `if (isLoading) return
;`. Risk: none behavioural; the tagged-union remodelling of `useLibrary`'s return belongs to F023 and should not be attempted here.

findings.title: User-controlled book titles are interpolated raw into the prompt that defines the requested output shape
findings.description: `recommendationsPrompt(booksList)` embeds a string that recommend.ts:20-22 builds from `b.title`, `b.author` and `b.category` for every book in the library, unescaped and unlength-capped. Those values are not app-authored: the Goodreads CSV importer writes them verbatim from a file the user supplies, and `Book.title`/`author`/`category` are plain `string` (src/types.ts:31-33) with no branding separating 'text safe to interpolate into a prompt' from 'arbitrary imported text'. The same pattern applies at prompts.ts:24 (detailedSummaryPrompt), :45 (quizPrompt), :56 (chatSystemInstruction) and :81 (audioScript), which additionally interpolate `summary.summary` and `summary.keyInsights` — themselves prior model output. Because line 41 asks in prose for 'strictly JSON with an array of objects containing title, author, and a 1-sentence description', a crafted title can restate or contradict that instruction and steer the response shape; combined with L05-F04's unvalidated cast, a steered response reaches the consumer as a typed `Recommendation[]`. This is adjacent to prompt injection but its type-safety consequence is concrete: the codebase treats a string that controls a request's output contract as interchangeable with a display string. Correct fix shape: escape or fence interpolated library values (and cap their length) in the prompt builders, and keep the runtime validation at the parse site as the real defence. Verified negative worth recording: prompts.ts is otherwise clean — every export has inferred-string return types from template literals, no assertions, no non-null assertions, and the `type: 'short' | 'long'` parameter at line 79 is a proper literal union. Blast radius: 5 prompt builders, all 6 AI entry points.
findings.verifierNote: The mechanics are exactly as described - prompts.ts:39-42 interpolates `booksList` raw, recommend.ts:20-22 builds it from unescaped, uncapped `b.title` / `b.author` / `b.category`, and the same raw interpolation occurs at prompts.ts:24, :45, :56 and :79, several of which also embed prior model output (`summary.summary`, `summary.keyInsights`). The verified negative is accurate too: prompts.ts has no assertions, no `!`, and :79's `type: 'short' | 'long'` is a proper literal union. But medium under boundary-without-validation overstates it on two counts. (1) Category: nothing external is being TYPED here - data flows OUT of typed code into a string, so no type is claiming correctness the runtime cannot deliver. The argument the finding actually makes ('a string that controls a request's output contract is interchangeable with a display string') is a branded-type argument, and the spec explicitly warns those belong only where the foot-gun cost is real. (2) Cost: BookSum is local-first with no server, no accounts and no other party's data - the 'attacker' supplies their own CSV and their own API key, so a crafted title can only steer the model into returning junk to the user who wrote it, and there is no exfiltration channel. The real defence the finding itself names - validating at the parse site - is already filed separately (the unvalidated Recommendation cast). Amended to low with the category corrected.
findings.reachability: A user imports a Goodreads CSV whose title field contains instructions, then refreshes recommendations. The steered response reaches the consumer as a typed `Recommendation[]`. No privilege boundary is crossed - the only affected party is the author of the input.
findings.blastRadius: 5 prompt builders (prompts.ts:24, :39, :45, :56, :79) fed by 1 unescaped join (recommend.ts:20-22).
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest effective step, in recommend.ts:20-22 rather than in every builder: `const clean = (s: string) => s.replace(/[\r\n]+/g, ' ').slice(0, 120); const booksList = userBooks.slice(0, 100).map((b) => `"${clean(b.title)}" by ${clean(b.author)} (${clean(b.category)})`).join(', ');`. The slice(0, 100) also caps prompt size for large imported libraries, which is the more likely real-world problem. Risk: truncation changes recommendation quality for very long titles - acceptable; keep the parse-site validation as the actual defence.
findings.amendedDescription: recommend.ts:20-22 builds the prompt fragment from unescaped, uncapped user-imported `title`/`author`/`category`, and prompts.ts:39-42 interpolates it directly above the sentence that defines the requested output shape; the same raw interpolation appears at prompts.ts:24, :45, :56 and :79. `Book.title` etc. are plain `string` (types.ts:31-33), with no distinction between 'display text' and 'text that steers a request contract'. In a local-first, single-user, no-server app this crosses no privilege boundary - the only party who can inject is the party who receives the output - so treat it as hygiene (escape newlines, cap length, cap the number of books to bound prompt size) and keep validation at the parse site as the real defence.

findings.title: pcmToWavBlob stamps a hardcoded 24kHz/mono/16-bit header on unvalidated Gemini bytes while discarding the mimeType the API actually returns
findings.description:
The signature `pcmToWavBlob(pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>): Blob` is type-correct but encodes a format contract that only a JSDoc comment asserts ('Gemini TTS returns headerless 24kHz mono 16-bit PCM'). SAMPLE_RATE, NUM_CHANNELS and BITS_PER_SAMPLE are module constants (lines 1-3) written into the header unconditionally. `Uint8Array` says nothing about sample rate, channel count, bit depth, or even that the byte count is even — which it must be for 16-bit mono, since an odd length yields a `data` chunk size that is not a multiple of `blockAlign` (2) and therefore a malformed final sample frame.

The bytes are unvalidated external data. `src/lib/ai/tts.ts:27` reads `response.candidates?.[0]?.content?.parts?.[0]?.inlineData?.data` and line 30 pipes it through `base64ToBytes` straight into `pcmToWavBlob`. Critically, the SDK's `inlineData` is `{ data?: string; displayName?: string; mimeType?: string }` (`node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts:1239-1247`) — the authoritative format IS returned by the API as `mimeType` (e.g. `audio/L16;rate=24000`), and the code discards it in favour of three hardcoded constants.

Failure mode is the dangerous kind: no exception, silently corrupt output.
