If Gemini ever returns a different rate or bit depth (a model or default change, a different voice pipeline), the header mislabels the stream and the browser plays the audio at the wrong speed and pitch, or as noise. Nothing in the type system, and nothing at runtime, would flag it.

Correct behaviour: read `inlineData.mimeType`, parse the declared rate/encoding, and either build the header from it or reject a stream that does not match the expected format; and reject an odd `pcm.length` for 16-bit audio.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the header arithmetic — I checked all 44 bytes against the RIFF/WAVE spec and they are correct: 'RIFF' at 0; ChunkSize `36 + pcm.length` at 4; 'WAVE' at 8; 'fmt ' (with trailing space) at 12; Subchunk1Size 16 at 16; AudioFormat 1 at 20; NumChannels 1 at 22; SampleRate 24000 at 24; ByteRate 48000 at 28 (= 24000*1*2); BlockAlign 2 at 32 (= 1*2); BitsPerSample 16 at 34; 'data' at 36; Subchunk2Size `pcm.length` at 40. All little-endian. `pcm.length` equals `byteLength` for a `Uint8Array`, so the two size fields are right. There are also NO type assertions anywhere in this file, and the parameter is correctly narrowed to `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` rather than asserting `as ArrayBuffer` over an `ArrayBufferLike`.

Blast radius: one call site (`src/lib/ai/tts.ts:30`), but it is the whole audio-summary feature.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present exactly as described: src/lib/audio/wav.ts:1-3 declares SAMPLE_RATE/NUM_CHANNELS/BITS_PER_SAMPLE as module constants and :12 takes `pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` carrying no format information. I re-checked the header arithmetic against the RIFF/WAVE spec and the finding's verified-negative holds: 'RIFF'@0, 36+len@4, 'WAVE'@8, 'fmt '@12, 16@16, 1@20, 1@22, 24000@24, 48000@28, 2@32, 16@34, 'data'@36, len@40, all little-endian. But this is the CONSUMER HALF of F081, not an independent defect: the discarded `mimeType` lives in tts.ts:27 and the only way to fix wav.ts is for tts.ts to pass the parsed format in. Counting it twice at medium double-weights one defect. wav.ts itself is an honest, correctly documented pure function (JSDoc at :11 states its contract), contains no assertions or non-null assertions, and has exactly one non-test caller. The one genuinely independent claim - that an odd `pcm.length` yields a data chunk that is not a multiple of blockAlign - is arithmetically true but has no producer that can emit it (16-bit PCM is always even-length) and no consequence beyond a truncated final frame.
findings.reachability: Same single path as F081 (tts.ts:30). No independent reachability: `pcmToWavBlob` is exported but has no other production importer.
findings.blastRadius: 1 non-test call site (src/lib/ai/tts.ts:30), plus src/lib/audio/wav.test.ts. Strictly smaller than F081's.
findings.suggestedPatch:
Fix once, at F081's site. If wav.ts is touched at all, widen the signature rather than adding a second validation layer:
  export function pcmToWavBlob(pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>, sampleRate = SAMPLE_RATE, channels = NUM_CHANNELS): Blob
and write those into the header instead of the constants. Risk: none to existing callers - both parameters default to today's values.
findings.amendedDescription: Duplicate of F081 filed against the consumer file. src/lib/audio/wav.ts:12 encodes a 24kHz/mono/16-bit format contract in module constants (lines 1-3) that its `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` parameter type cannot express, and stamps it unconditionally into the RIFF header at lines 23-27. The bytes are unvalidated Gemini output, but the field that would validate them (`inlineData.mimeType`) is discarded upstream at src/lib/ai/tts.ts:27, which is where the fix belongs. wav.ts has one non-test caller, its header arithmetic is verified correct against the RIFF spec, and it contains no type assertions or non-null assertions. Track as the consumer half of F081; do not count as a second medium.

findings.title: Redundant `bytes[i] as number` pre-suppresses exactly the check noUncheckedIndexedAccess would add
findings.description:
Under the current `tsconfig.json` (strict: true, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` NOT set), indexing a `Uint8Array` already yields `number` via its numeric index signature, so `as number` is a no-op assertion that the compiler does not need. It is not currently hiding a bug — the loop bound `i < bytes.length` makes every index provably in range.

It matters for a specific forward-looking reason that is squarely this audit's concern: if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled (a likely structural recommendation for this repo, since it is otherwise clean under strict), this cast is precisely the construct that would make the new flag a silent no-op at this site instead of surfacing the indexed-access question. A cast that exists only to pre-empt a strictness flag is indistinguishable from one that is masking a real out-of-bounds read, and a reviewer cannot tell them apart without re-deriving the loop bound.

Correct fix shape: delete the assertion (it is unnecessary today), and if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is later enabled, restructure the loop with `for (const byte of bytes)` so the element type is `number` without any assertion.

Blast radius: one line, internal to this module. `bytesToBase64` itself has no production caller — grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/base64.test.ts`.
findings.verifierNote: Present verbatim at base64.ts:17 `binary += String.fromCharCode(bytes[i] as number);`. Under the current tsconfig, `Uint8Array`'s numeric index signature already yields `number`, so the assertion is a no-op the compiler does not need, and the loop bound at :16 (`i < bytes.length`) makes every index provably in range - so it is masking nothing today. It is a real instance of the audit's concern all the same: a cast whose only effect is to pre-empt `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is indistinguishable, on review, from one masking a genuine out-of-bounds read. Blast radius re-verified by grep: `bytesToBase64` is imported only by src/lib/base64.test.ts (:2, :7) and has zero production callers, which is why `low` is right.
findings.reachability: Test-only today (the base64.test.ts round-trip). `base64ToBytes`, the sibling that does have a production caller via migrate.ts:136, contains no such cast.
findings.blastRadius: 1 line, 1 module, 0 production call sites.
findings.suggestedPatch: Restructure the loop so no assertion is needed under any flag: `for (const byte of bytes) binary += String.fromCharCode(byte);` replacing :16-18. Risk: none - `target: ES2022` with `lib: ["ES2022", "DOM", ...]` supports iterating a TypedArray directly, and iteration order is identical.

findings.title: relativeLuminance accepts any string and returns NaN or a plausible wrong number, defeating the project's own WCAG guardrail
findings.description:
`relativeLuminance(hex: string): number` accepts any `string` and declares it always yields a `number`. There is no format validation: `hex.replace('#','')` then `parseInt(slice, 16)` on three fixed slices. Verified at runtime against real inputs:

- `'white'`, `'rgb(255,255,255)'`, `'var(--x)'`, `'oklch(0.7 0.2 40)'`, `''` and 4-digit `#RGBA` shorthand `'#f00a'` all produce `NaN` channels -> `relativeLuminance` returns `NaN` -> `contrastRatio` returns `NaN`.
- Worse, a 5-digit typo `'#12345'` produces NO NaN at all: `parseInt('5', 16)` = 5, so it returns a confident, plausible, wrong luminance (0.0260) and a wrong ratio (1.519 vs `#000000`). A one-character typo in a colour token yields a silently wrong pass/fail verdict with no signal whatsoever.

Why it matters specifically here: CLAUDE.md designates this file as the project's WCAG AA guardrail ('src/lib/contrast.ts exists to assert colour choices meet WCAG AA. Use it when changing colours.'). A guardrail that silently accepts bad input defeats its own purpose. And because `NaN < 4.5` is `false`, any guard written in the natural direction — `if (contrastRatio(fg, bg) < 4.5) fail()` — silently PASSES on unparseable input. The one thing that limits blast radius today is that the module has no production caller: grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/contrast.test.ts`, and Vitest's `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual` / `toBeLessThan` both fail on NaN, so the current tests would notice. That protection evaporates the moment the module is used in app code or someone writes a guard-style check.

Correct behaviour: parse into `number | null` (or accept a branded `HexColor` produced by one validating constructor) so an unsupported format is a type error or an explicit failure rather than a number. Supporting `#RGBA`/`#RRGGBBAA` and rejecting any other length would close the silent-wrong-value case.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the maths itself: the WCAG 2.1 formula is correct — sRGB linearisation threshold 0.03928 with `/12.92` and `((c+0.055)/1.055)**2.4`, coefficients 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722, and `(lighter+0.05)/(darker+0.05)`. `#000000` vs `#ffffff` yields exactly 21. Only the parsing is unsound.
findings.verifierNote: Every runtime claim reproduces. I ran the exact implementation from src/lib/contrast.ts:8-23: 'white' -> NaN, '' -> NaN, 'rgb(255,255,255)' -> NaN, '#f00a' -> NaN, and the silent-wrong-value case '#12345' -> luminance 0.02595538497129003 with contrastRatio('#12345','#000000') = 1.5191076994258006. The WCAG maths is correct (#000000 vs #ffffff = exactly 21) and `NaN < 4.5` is `false`, so a guard written in the natural direction silently passes. All true. What does not hold at medium is impact: I grepped the whole tree and src/lib/contrast.ts is imported by exactly one file, src/lib/contrast.test.ts. There is ZERO production call site, so there is no path on which a wrong value can arrive and compile - the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. Per the spec's scale that is 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents', i.e. low. The finding's own text already concedes the module has no production caller, so the severity was set above what its evidence supports.
findings.reachability: Not reachable from the running app. Only src/lib/contrast.test.ts imports it, and Vitest's toBeGreaterThanOrEqual/toBeLessThan both fail on NaN, so a NaN would be caught today. The '#12345' silent-wrong-number case would NOT be caught by a test that only asserts a threshold. Re-rate to medium if a production caller ever lands, which CLAUDE.md invites ('use it when changing colours').
findings.blastRadius: 1 importer, and it is a test file. 0 production call sites (verified by grep over src/).
findings.amendedDescription: src/lib/contrast.ts:8 `relativeLuminance(hex: string): number` accepts any string and its `number` return type is a lie for unparseable input: verified at runtime, 'white'/''/'rgb(...)'/'#f00a' all yield NaN, and a 5-digit typo '#12345' yields a confident wrong luminance (0.0260) and wrong ratio (1.519) with no signal. Because `NaN < 4.5` is false, a guard written in the natural direction silently passes. The WCAG maths itself is verified correct. Lowered to low because the module has no production caller whatsoever - src/lib/contrast.test.ts is its only importer - so no incident is reachable today.

findings.title: mockFetch types every API fixture as unknown, so no fixture is checked against the as-asserted response shapes
findings.description:
`mockFetch(handler: (url: string) => unknown)` returns `unknown`, so every response fixture in this file — `{ items: [{ volumeInfo: { imageLinks: { large } } }] }` on line 24, `{ docs: [{ cover_i: 12345 }] }` on line 36 — is invisible to the compiler. Those two assertions at `googleBooks.ts:12-14` and `openLibrary.ts:6` are the ONLY types the app has for two external HTTP APIs, and the tests that are supposed to pin them cannot detect drift between fixture and assertion in either direction.

Concrete gaps this creates:
- `googleBooks.ts:13` types `imageLinks?: Record<string, string>`. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (measured baseline), `links.extraLarge` is typed `string` — non-optional — while at runtime it is `undefined` for the vast majority of Google Books volumes, which return only `thumbnail`/`smallThumbnail`. The `??` chain on lines 19-23 works by accident of runtime `undefined`, not because the type says so. No fixture exercises an `imageLinks` object missing `large`, so the fallback ladder below line 20 is never executed by any test.
- No fixture produces a 200 with a non-JSON body, even though `mockFetch` can: a handler returning `undefined` makes `JSON.stringify(result)` evaluate to `undefined`, yielding a 200 with an empty body, and `response.json()` then throws `SyntaxError` — swallowed silently by the bare `catch {}` at `index.ts:17`, which would degrade every cover to a placeholder with no signal.
- No fixture exercises `items: [{}]` (an entry with no `volumeInfo`) or `docs: [{}]` (no `cover_i`).

What goes untested: the whole malformed/partial-response half of two `as`-asserted boundaries, plus the `Record<string, string>` claim that every key is a present string.
findings.verifierNote: Claims verified: src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:5 is `function mockFetch(handler: (url: string) => unknown)`, so the fixtures at :24 (`{ items: [{ volumeInfo: { imageLinks: { large } } }] }`), :36 (`{ docs: [{ cover_i: 12345 }] }`) and :46 are never checked against the assertions at googleBooks.ts:12-14 and openLibrary.ts:6; no fixture supplies `items: [{}]`, `docs: [{}]`, an `imageLinks` lacking `large`, or a non-JSON 200 body. AMENDED DOWN two steps to low, for three reasons. (1) Inverted ranking: the production-side findings this mirrors — F085 (googleBooks.ts:12) and F086 (openLibrary.ts:6) — are both `medium`, and F111 already carries the `Record<string, string>` lie; a test mirror cannot outrank its producers. (2) Blast radius is cosmetic and fully absorbed: src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-21 wraps both lookups in `try { ... } catch {}` and returns `placeholderCover(title)`, so every untested path — malformed body, missing `imageLinks` key, missing `cover_i` — degrades to a locally generated SVG placeholder. No crash, no persistence, no data corruption; the worst outcome is a book showing initials instead of a cover. (3) Minor imprecision in the write-up: the code reads `links?.extraLarge` (googleBooks.ts:19), so the expression type is already `string | undefined` via the optional chain; the index-signature lie is real but is F111's finding, not this one. I am deliberately not applying a reflexive test-file downgrade — the spec warns against that — but the severity scale explicitly places weak types in test fixtures at low when the blast radius is cosmetic, and here it is.
findings.reachability: No runtime path of its own. The gaps it leaves untested are all swallowed by the `catch {}` at src/lib/covers/index.ts:17 and end in `placeholderCover`.
findings.blastRadius: One test helper with 3 call sites inside a single 88-line test file; the boundary it fails to pin has 2 assertion sites (googleBooks.ts:12, openLibrary.ts:6) whose only output is a cover-image URL string.
findings.amendedDescription: `mockFetch` (src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:5) types its handler's return as `unknown`, so none of the response fixtures (lines 24, 36, 46) is checked against the `as`-asserted shapes at googleBooks.ts:12-14 and openLibrary.ts:6, and drift between fixture and assertion is undetectable in either direction. No fixture exercises `items: [{}]`, `docs: [{}]`, an `imageLinks` object lacking `large`, or a 200 with a non-JSON body. Severity lowered to low: this is the test mirror of F085/F086 (both medium — a test mirror should not outrank its producers), and every untested path is absorbed by the `try/catch {}` in src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-21, whose worst outcome is a locally generated placeholder cover rather than a crash or a bad write. (Minor correction: the code uses `links?.extraLarge`, so the expression already types as `string | undefined`; the `Record<string, string>` index-signature lie is tracked as F111.)

findings.title: Truthy check on a numeric cover id conflates absent with zero
findings.description:
`coverId` is `number | undefined` and L8 tests it with a bare truthy check, so a cover id of `0` is treated identically to a missing one. This is the textbook `0`-is-falsy coercion bug: the intent is unmistakably 'did we get an id?', but the expression asks 'is the id non-zero?'. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: `typeof coverId === 'number'` (which also happens to close the L06-F02 validation hole in the same edit) or at minimum `coverId !== undefined`.

CONCRETE FAILURE: a record whose `cover_i` is `0` returns `null`, `fetchCover` falls through to `placeholderCover`, and the user gets a generated initials tile instead of the real cover. No crash and no data corruption — the failure is a silently-degraded image, which is why this is low.

NOTE ON THE SAME LINE IN THE SAME FUNCTION: the identical pattern appears at src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:24 (`if (url) return ...`), where the truthy check is on a `string` and correctly rejects `''`. That one is fine; only the numeric case is wrong.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present at openLibrary.ts:7-8: `const coverId = data.docs?.[0]?.cover_i;` then `return coverId ? ... : null;` on a value declared `number | undefined`. That is textbook numeric truthiness and the category is right. The CONCRETE FAILURE claim does not survive, which is why this is amended down to hygiene-only: for `cover_i === 0` to cost the user a real cover, id 0 would have to address a real image in OpenLibrary's cover-id space, which is a positive auto-increment - and even if such a record existed, I traced the consumer: `fetchCover` (covers/index.ts:12-22) treats a falsy return identically to a thrown error and falls through to `placeholderCover(title)`, which is the same tile a 404 on `/b/id/0-L.jpg` would produce after BookCard's `onError` swap. The two paths are indistinguishable to the user, so there is no realizable degradation - just an expression that asks the wrong question. The finding's own note that googleBooks.ts:24's `if (url)` on a `string` is fine is correct (I read :18-28; the empty-string case is desirable there).
findings.reachability: Called from `fetchCover` on every cover lookup that Google Books misses. Reached often; the falsy-zero branch is not reachable with real OpenLibrary data.
findings.blastRadius: 1 expression, 1 module, 1 caller (covers/index.ts:13).
findings.suggestedPatch: openLibrary.ts:8 -> `return typeof coverId === 'number' ? `https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/${coverId}-L.jpg` : null;`. Risk: none, and it additionally rejects a non-number `cover_i` arriving from the unvalidated `as` cast at :6.
findings.amendedDescription: `coverId` is `number | undefined` and openLibrary.ts:8 tests it with a bare truthy check, so a cover id of `0` is treated as absent. The pattern is a genuine numeric-truthiness smell and the one-token fix is worth taking, but the user-visible failure originally claimed is not realizable: OpenLibrary cover ids are positive, and `fetchCover` (covers/index.ts:12-22) already maps a `null` return and a 404 image to the same `placeholderCover` outcome. Hygiene only.

findings.title: download.test.ts covers only slugify; downloadText has no return annotation and cannot run under the current harness
findings.description:
The module exports two functions. Only `slugify` is tested, and it is tested well (5 cases including the empty-result fallback and the length cap). `downloadText` — the function that actually performs the user-visible export — has zero coverage and cannot be given any without harness work.

`download.ts:2` declares `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` with no return type annotation, on an exported symbol. More importantly it calls `URL.createObjectURL` (line 4) and `URL.revokeObjectURL` (line 11). jsdom does not implement either, and `src/test/setup.ts` stubs neither, so any test touching this path dies with `TypeError: URL.createObjectURL is not a function`. `lib.dom` declares both as unconditionally present, so the compiler asserts a capability the test environment does not have — the ambient type is a lie about the runtime the suite runs in.

The same gap blocks three other production call sites: `ProfileView.tsx:99` (library JSON export), `BookDetail.tsx:160` (TTS playback) and `:199` (PDF open), and `EReader.tsx:204`. `useTheme.test.tsx:28` demonstrates the pattern for the analogous `matchMedia` gap by stubbing it per-file rather than in `setup.ts`.

What goes untested: the entire download/blob-URL surface, including the `revokeObjectURL` cleanup that prevents leaked object URLs.
findings.verifierNote: Two problems with the finding as filed. First, misattribution: it is filed at src/lib/download.test.ts:1, but the cited pattern is at src/lib/download.ts:2, `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')`. I read all 24 lines of the test file; it contains no type weakness, only five clean `slugify` cases. Second, calibration: the only type-safety content is a missing return-type annotation on an exported function whose body has no `return` statement, so the inferred return type is exactly `void`. That is not an implicit `any`, it degrades no caller, and `noImplicitAny` correctly does not fire. Both parameters ARE annotated and `mimeType` is inferred `string` from its default. That is hygiene, i.e. low. Everything else in the finding - jsdom not implementing `URL.createObjectURL`, zero coverage of the download surface, the untested `revokeObjectURL` cleanup - is a test-coverage argument, which this audit's scope assigns elsewhere. Real gap, wrong audit, wrong severity.
findings.reachability: `downloadText` is reachable from production (markdown export at src/components/ProfileView.tsx:92, plus the BookDetail/EReader blob paths), but the missing `: void` has no runtime consequence anywhere - there is no value to mis-consume.
findings.blastRadius: 4 non-test call sites of `downloadText`. The type weakness itself has a blast radius of zero: `void` is inferred precisely, so no consumer is degraded.
findings.amendedDescription: Filed against the wrong file: the pattern is at src/lib/download.ts:2, not src/lib/download.test.ts:1. `downloadText` is an exported function with no return-type annotation; its parameters ARE annotated and its inferred return is exactly `void`, so no caller degrades and no implicit `any` is introduced. Adding `: void` is a one-line hygiene fix. The finding's substantive content - that the whole download/blob-URL surface is untested because jsdom does not implement `URL.createObjectURL` and src/test/setup.ts does not stub it - is a genuine coverage gap but belongs to a testing audit, not this one.

findings.title: downloadText takes three adjacent bare-string positional params, so swapping filename and contents compiles cleanly
findings.description:
`downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` has three same-typed positional parameters where order is entirely load-bearing and the compiler cannot distinguish them. `downloadText(markdown, filename)` type-checks and silently produces a download whose filename is the entire markdown body (browsers truncate/sanitise it) containing the filename as its content. This is the classic branded-type foot-gun from the audit spec's red-team list.

The risk is live because both call sites build the two arguments inline in the same expression and could easily be transposed during a refactor: `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:92` — `downloadText(\`booksum-library-${new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0]}.md\`, markdown)` — and `src/components/BookDetail.tsx:417` — `downloadText(\`${slugify(book.title)}.md\`, bookToMarkdown(book, summary))`.

`mimeType` is likewise a bare `string` interpolated into a Content-Type at line 3 (`\`${mimeType};charset=utf-8\``); passing an already-parameterised value such as `'text/csv;charset=iso-8859-1'` would emit a double `charset` with no type error. No current call site does.

Correct behaviour: take a single options object (`{ filename, contents, mimeType }`), or brand `Filename` / `MimeType`. An options object is the cheaper fix here and removes the ordering hazard entirely.

VERIFIED NEGATIVES for this file: `document.createElement('a')` is correctly used without a cast (it already returns `HTMLAnchorElement`), there are no element or DOM type assertions anywhere in the file, and `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` IS called (line 11), so there is no object-URL leak. `slugify`'s `|| 'untitled'` at line 21 is a truthy check on a string where the empty-string branch is the intended behaviour, not a coercion bug.

Blast radius: 2 call sites.
findings.verifierNote: Signature present verbatim at download.ts:2 `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')`, with `filename` reaching `anchor.download` (:7) and `contents` reaching `new Blob([contents], ...)` (:3). Both call sites verified by grep and both build the two arguments inline in a single expression - ProfileView.tsx:92 and BookDetail.tsx:417 - so a transposition during a refactor is exactly the ordering hazard the spec's red-team list names ('function signatures with multiple same-typed parameters where order matters'). `downloadText(markdown, filename)` type-checks. The `mimeType` sub-point is weaker and should be treated as secondary: no call site passes it, so the double-`charset` scenario is hypothetical. The file's verified negatives also hold: `document.createElement('a')` is used without a cast and `URL.revokeObjectURL` is called at :11.
findings.reachability: Both call sites are user-triggered exports (library backup, single-book markdown). Live code; no current call site is transposed.
findings.blastRadius: 1 exported function, 2 production call sites, 0 tests.
findings.suggestedPatch: Collapse to one options object: `export function downloadText({ filename, contents, mimeType = 'text/markdown' }: { filename: string; contents: string; mimeType?: string })`, and update ProfileView.tsx:92 / BookDetail.tsx:417 to named form. Risk: only 2 call sites, but it is an API-shape change - do it in one commit so no caller is left on the positional form.

findings.title: coverForIsbn is tested with one perfect ISBN and undefined, so unvalidated ISBN text becomes Book.coverImageUrl
findings.description:
The `coverForIsbn` block has exactly two cases: a clean 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`. `GoodreadsRow.isbn13?: string` is unvalidated free text — `cleanIsbn` at `goodreads.ts:69-72` only strips the Goodreads `="..."` wrapper and returns whatever remains if it is non-empty. `coverForIsbn` then interpolates that directly into a URL and its `string | undefined` return type says nothing about whether the URL resolves.

`useLibrary.tsx:158` writes the result into a `Book`: `coverImageUrl: coverForIsbn(row.isbn13) ?? placeholderCover(row.title)`. Because a bad ISBN still yields a truthy string, the `??` placeholder fallback is bypassed and the book is persisted with a permanently-broken cover URL. Real Goodreads exports produce exactly the inputs no fixture covers: hyphenated ISBNs (`="978-0-7352-1129-2"` -> `covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/978-0-7352-1129-2-L.jpg`), 10-digit ISBNs, and placeholder values such as `="0"`. `Book.coverImageUrl: string` claims a usable image URL and delivers an arbitrary string.

What goes untested: every non-canonical ISBN shape, and the interaction that decides whether a Goodreads-imported book gets a real cover or a dead link.

Verified sound in the rest of this file: the `parseGoodreadsCsv` block (lines 10-93) is the strongest suite in the lot — it covers quoted commas, doubled quotes, embedded newlines, CRLF, column reordering, a missing optional column, and the skipped counter. The only gap there is that a blank interior line also increments `skipped` (parseCsv emits a `['']` row, whose empty title takes the skip branch at `goodreads.ts:99-102`), inflating the count shown to the user.
findings.verifierNote: The described state of the tests is exactly right: src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:95-105 has precisely two `coverForIsbn` cases, a clean 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`. The underlying behaviour is real too - src/lib/goodreads.ts:69-72 `cleanIsbn` only strips the `="..."` wrapper via `replace(/^="?|"?$/g, '')` and returns whatever remains if non-empty, then :121-122 interpolates it unconditionally, so src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 `coverForIsbn(row.isbn13) ?? placeholderCover(row.title)` never reaches the `??` for a truthy-but-garbage ISBN. What does not hold up is medium. (a) It is filed as `branded-type-opportunity` on a TEST file, but there is no call site where a wrong value arrives and compiles into something the compiler could have caught - `string | undefined` is an honest description of what `coverForIsbn` returns, so the branded-type framing does not apply. (b) I verified the user-visible impact is nil: src/components/BookCard.tsx defines `handleError` which sets `placeholderCover(book.title)` on image load failure, plus a `useEffect` that pre-empts empty/'null' URLs, so a dead OpenLibrary URL renders as exactly the placeholder the `??` would have produced, one failed request later.
findings.reachability: Reachable on any Goodreads import containing hyphenated, 10-digit or placeholder ISBNs, which real exports do contain. Outcome: one wasted image request per affected book, then the placeholder renders. No crash, no wrong data displayed.
findings.blastRadius: 1 non-test call site of `coverForIsbn` (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158). The value lands in `Book.coverImageUrl` and is read only by BookCard's guarded ``.
findings.amendedDescription: src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:95-105 tests `coverForIsbn` with only a canonical 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`, leaving every real-world Goodreads ISBN shape (hyphenated, 10-digit, placeholder '0') uncovered. Those inputs do produce a truthy but dead cover URL that bypasses the `?? placeholderCover(...)` fallback at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 and is persisted to `Book.coverImageUrl`. Lowered to low: the return type `string | undefined` is honest and no wrong value can compile where the compiler could have helped, and src/components/BookCard.tsx's `handleError` swaps in the same placeholder on load failure, so the end state is identical to the intended fallback. Worth fixing for correctness hygiene, not for incident risk.

findings.title: `columnOf` returns a bare `number` hiding a `-1` not-found sentinel that no type can narrow
findings.description:
`columnOf` (L83) has no return annotation and infers `number` from `Array.prototype.indexOf`, so the `-1` not-found sentinel is completely invisible in the type. All six derived constants (L85-90 `titleAt`, `authorAt`, `ratingAt`, `shelfAt`, `isbnAt`, `dateReadAt`) are typed `number`, and 'column 3' and 'column not present' are indistinguishable to the compiler. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: return `number | null` (or a small `{found: true, index} | {found: false}` union) so consumers must narrow before indexing.

CONCRETE FAILURE 1 (footgun, latent): index `0` is a valid column AND is falsy. The current `cell()` helper checks `index >= 0` correctly, but any future refactor to the idiomatic-looking `if (titleAt)` silently drops the column-0 case — which the repo's own test at src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:67 exercises (`'Title,Author,Exclusive Shelf\nDune,Herbert,read'`, Title at index 0). The type gives no hint that `0` is meaningful.

CONCRETE FAILURE 2 (live, user-visible): when the `title` header is absent entirely — a non-Goodreads CSV, or an export with localised/renamed headers — `titleAt` is `-1`, `cell(-1)` returns `''` for every row, so every row hits the `if (!title)` branch at L99 and increments `skipped`. The user sees '0 books found' (GoodreadsImport.tsx:27-29) plus 'N rows skipped' with no indication that the problem is a missing header rather than an empty file. A narrowable return type would force this case to be handled explicitly at the top of the function.

BLAST RADIUS: 6 call sites inside this file; no external consumers.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern confirmed at goodreads.ts:83 `const columnOf = (name: string) => header.indexOf(name.toLowerCase());` - no return annotation, infers `number`, and the `-1` not-found sentinel is invisible in the type across all six derived constants (:85-90). The falsy-zero footgun is real and the repo's own test proves index 0 is meaningful: goodreads.test.ts:66-70 ('tolerates a missing optional column') parses `'Title,Author,Exclusive Shelf\nDune,Herbert,read'`, where Title is column 0; a future refactor to `if (titleAt)` would silently break it, and only `cell`'s `index >= 0` check at :96 keeps it correct today. CONCRETE FAILURE 2 is overstated and is the reason for the amendment: I read the consumer, and when the title header is missing the user does NOT get an unexplained result - GoodreadsImport.tsx shows `toast.error('No books found in that file. Is it a Goodreads CSV export?')`, which names the likely cause. So the user-facing consequence is a correct-but-imprecise message, not a silent dead end. Severity stays `low`.
findings.reachability: Every CSV import. The `-1` path is reachable with any non-Goodreads or localised-header CSV, and is handled correctly at runtime by :96 - the weakness is that nothing in the type enforces that handling.
findings.blastRadius: 6 uses inside this file (:85-90 feeding :98-113). `columnOf` is a function-local arrow, not exported - no external consumers.
findings.suggestedPatch: `const columnOf = (name: string): number | null => { const index = header.indexOf(name.toLowerCase()); return index >= 0 ? index : null; };` and `const cell = (index: number | null) => (index === null ? '' : (cells[index] ?? '').trim());`. Risk: none - all six consumers go through `cell`, and the compiler will flag any that does not.
findings.amendedDescription: `columnOf` (goodreads.ts:83) has no return annotation and infers `number` from `Array.prototype.indexOf`, so the `-1` not-found sentinel is invisible in the type and all six derived column constants (:85-90) make 'column 3' and 'column absent' indistinguishable to the compiler. Index `0` is both a valid column and falsy, and the repo's own test at goodreads.test.ts:66-70 exercises Title at index 0, so a refactor to the idiomatic-looking `if (titleAt)` would silently drop it - only the `index >= 0` check inside `cell` (:96) makes the current code correct, and the type does not require it. The originally-claimed user-facing failure is softer than stated: when the title header is missing entirely, GoodreadsImport already surfaces 'No books found in that file. Is it a Goodreads CSV export?', so the user is pointed at the right cause even though the parser cannot distinguish the case internally.

findings.title: `dateRead` is parsed and typed as `string` with no format contract, then silently discarded
findings.description:
`GoodreadsRow.dateRead?: string` (L9) is populated at L113 from raw file content with zero validation — no format check, no parse, no `isNaN(d.getTime())` guard. Two distinct problems.

PROBLEM 1 (live, and the reason this is only low): the field has NO consumer. `importGoodreadsRows` (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:150-160) maps `title`, `author`, `status`, `rating` and `isbn13` but never reads `dateRead`, so `Book.finishedAt` is left `undefined` for every imported book — including books imported as `'Finished'`. A repo-wide grep confirms `finishedAt` is declared at src/types.ts:40 and written NOWHERE in `src/`. The exported type therefore advertises data the pipeline discards, which is a type-honesty defect: a consumer reading `GoodreadsParseResult` reasonably concludes read-dates survive the import. They do not.

PROBLEM 2 (latent, and the brief's `Invalid Date` hypothesis): because nothing consumes it, there is currently NO `new Date(csvString)` anywhere in this lot — VERIFIED NEGATIVE. But the moment someone wires it up, Goodreads writes this column as `YYYY/MM/DD`, which is NOT an ISO-8601 form and is parsed inconsistently across engines; `new Date('2023/05/14')` is engine- and locale-dependent, and a blank or malformed cell yields `Invalid Date` — which is STILL typed `Date`, propagating a silently-broken value into `Book.finishedAt` and any date arithmetic downstream. The repo contains no `isNaN(getTime())` validation anywhere to catch it.

CORRECT BEHAVIOR: either drop the field from `GoodreadsRow` (it is dead weight that misleads), or validate it into an ISO date string at the parse boundary and actually map it to `Book.finishedAt`.
findings.verifierNote: The facts are all verified, but the framing overstates the type weakness. Confirmed: `dateRead?: string` is declared at goodreads.ts:9 and populated at :113 `dateRead: dateRead || undefined` from a raw CSV cell. Repo-wide grep confirms `dateRead` appears only in goodreads.ts (:9, :90, :105, :113) and goodreads.test.ts:22 - `importGoodreadsRows` (useLibrary.tsx:150-160) maps title/author/category/status/rating/coverImageUrl/hasPdf and never reads it - and `finishedAt` appears ONLY at its declaration, types.ts:40, with zero readers and zero writers in src/. So the real, provable defect is a dead field on both ends of the pipeline, not a validation gap: `string` is the honest type for 'whatever was in that CSV cell', and there is no consumer whose assumption it violates. PROBLEM 2 (the `new Date('2023/05/14')` hazard) is explicitly contingent on future code the finding itself confirms does not exist - it should be recorded as a note attached to any future wiring-up, not as a present-tense boundary finding. Severity `low` is right.
findings.reachability: Not reachable as a defect: no code reads `GoodreadsRow.dateRead` or writes `Book.finishedAt`. The only cost today is a misleading exported type.
findings.blastRadius: 2 declared-but-unused fields (goodreads.ts:9, types.ts:40); 1 write site (:113); 0 readers.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest and YAGNI-consistent: delete `dateRead?: string` (goodreads.ts:9), the `dateReadAt` lookup (:90), the local at :105 and the field at :113, and drop the `dateRead` expectation in goodreads.test.ts:22. Risk: if the intent is to keep the data, the alternative is to validate it into an ISO string at :113 and map it to `Book.finishedAt` in useLibrary.tsx:150-160 - do one or the other, not neither.
findings.amendedDescription: `GoodreadsRow.dateRead` (goodreads.ts:9) is parsed at :113 and never consumed by anything - `importGoodreadsRows` (useLibrary.tsx:150-160) drops it - and its natural destination, `Book.finishedAt` (types.ts:40), is declared with zero writers and zero readers repo-wide. The defect is therefore a type-honesty one of the dead-declaration kind: the exported parse result advertises data the pipeline discards, so a consumer reasonably concludes read-dates survive an import. There is no present validation gap, because nothing consumes the value and `string` is the honest type for a raw CSV cell. The `YYYY/MM/DD` parsing hazard (Goodreads' format is not ISO-8601 and `new Date` handling of it is engine-dependent, with `Invalid Date` still typed `Date`) is a note to attach to any future wiring-up, not a present-tense finding.

findings.title: `isbn13` is an unvalidated bare `string` interpolated unencoded into a persisted cover URL
findings.description: `cleanIsbn` (L69-72) strips Goodreads' `="..."` spreadsheet armour and returns whatever is left, typed as `isbn13?: string` (L8). Nothing checks it is 13 characters, or digits, or an ISBN at all — the name is the only thing asserting the domain. `coverForIsbn` (L121) then takes a bare `string | undefined` and interpolates it into a URL WITHOUT `encodeURIComponent`. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: a branded `Isbn13` type produced by a validating parser (`/^\d{13}$/`), plus `encodeURIComponent` at the interpolation site. CONCRETE FAILURE 1 (type mix-up — the classic branded-type footgun): `coverForIsbn(isbn13: string | undefined)` accepts ANY string, so `coverForIsbn(row.title)` type-checks perfectly and produces a garbage URL. Same-typed primitives with distinct domains are exactly what branding prevents. CONCRETE FAILURE 2 (live data quality): a 10-digit ISBN, an ASIN, or an ISSN passes through untouched and yields a 404 cover; an ISBN cell containing a space, `#`, `?`, or `/` (hand-edited CSV, or a mis-detected column) produces a malformed URL. That URL is PERSISTED to `Book.coverImageUrl` in IndexedDB at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 and later rendered as an ``, so the bad value outlives the import session and is only masked by BookCard's `onError` placeholder swap (src/components/BookCard.tsx:18/27). SECURITY BOUNDING (checked, deliberately not overclaimed): the value is interpolated after a fixed `https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/` path prefix, so it cannot change origin, and it lands in an `img src` rather than a script context — this is a data-quality and URL-correctness issue, not an SSRF or XSS one. VERIFIED CORRECT: the `/^="?|"?$/g` regex does handle Goodreads' real formats — `="9780735211292"` -> `9780735211292`, `=""` -> `''` -> `undefined` (matching the test at src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:27), and a bare ISBN passes through unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: Both halves verified in the current source. `cleanIsbn` (goodreads.ts:69-72) strips the `="..."` armour and returns whatever remains with no digit, length, or checksum test; `coverForIsbn` (:121-123) takes a bare `string | undefined` and interpolates it into a URL with no `encodeURIComponent`. The mixup is concretely available at the one production call site: useLibrary.tsx:158 `coverForIsbn(row.isbn13)` sits six lines below `title: row.title` (:152) in the same object literal, and `coverForIsbn(row.title)` would type-check exactly the same - this is the 'wrong value could actually arrive and compile' bar the spec sets for a branded-type finding, and it is met. The persistence claim also holds: the produced URL is written to `Book.coverImageUrl` at :158 and outlives the session, masked only by BookCard's `onError`. The finding's security bounding is correct and appropriately not overclaimed (fixed origin and path prefix, `img src` context). The verified-correct note on the regex matches the tests at goodreads.test.ts:12-23 and :47-49.
findings.reachability: Every Goodreads import with an ISBN column. A 10-digit ISBN, ASIN, or hand-edited cell reaches the URL builder unchecked and is persisted.
findings.blastRadius: 1 exported function, 1 production call site (useLibrary.tsx:158), 2 tests; the bad value is persisted to IndexedDB so its lifetime exceeds the call.
findings.suggestedPatch: Validate where the value is produced rather than branding every consumer: goodreads.ts:70-71 -> `const digits = (raw ?? '').replace(/^="?|"?$/g, '').trim(); return /^\d{13}$/.test(digits) ? digits : undefined;`. Risk: this now drops 10-digit ISBNs, so those rows fall back to `placeholderCover` at useLibrary.tsx:158 - acceptable, and the existing tests are unaffected (the only non-empty fixture ISBN is the 13-digit 9780735211292).

findings.title: Summary fixture always supplies real arrays, so the one consumer that would crash on an AI-shaped Summary is never exercised
findings.description:
The `summary` fixture is annotated `: Summary`, which is the right pattern and forces field completeness — but every array field is a hand-written real array (`keyInsights: ['Systems beat goals.', 'Identity drives habit.']`, `actionableSteps: ['Habit stack.']`), and the only variation the suite tries is the EMPTY array on line 70. Nothing in the lot ever hands `bookToMarkdown` a `Summary` whose fields came from `JSON.parse(...) as RawBookResponse`.

That matters because `markdown.ts` is the crash site for the untyped AI boundary. `summarize.ts:36` builds `keyInsights: data.keyInsights ?? []` from an unvalidated model response; `??` passes a string straight through. `markdown.ts:24-25` then does `if (summary.keyInsights.length > 0) { ...summary.keyInsights.map((i) => `- ${i}`) }` — a non-empty string satisfies `.length > 0` and then throws `TypeError: summary.keyInsights.map is not a function`, killing the library export. `markdown.ts:27-28` has the identical shape for `actionableSteps`.

So the type says `keyInsights: string[]`, the producer never checks, and the consumer's only tests supply values that make the claim true by construction. What goes untested: `bookToMarkdown`/`libraryToMarkdown` against any `Summary` that came off the wire rather than out of the test file. (The fixture itself is otherwise exemplary — explicitly annotated, complete, and the `Book` fixture on lines 5-18 likewise.)
findings.verifierNote: Claims are accurate: src/lib/markdown.test.ts:20-29 declares `const summary: Summary` with real arrays at :25-26, and the only variation the suite tries is the empty array at :70; src/lib/markdown.ts:24-25 and :27-28 do `if (x.length > 0) { ... x.map(...) }`, which a non-empty string would pass and then throw on. But the finding argues against itself. AMENDED DOWN to low for three reasons. (1) The fixture is annotated `: Summary` and complete — the finding says so itself ('otherwise exemplary'). Writing the missing test would require `as unknown as Summary` to smuggle a wire-shaped value past the compiler, which this same audit flags as `double-cast-as-unknown-as-T`; you cannot ask a suite to test a state its types forbid without introducing the exact defect class under audit. (2) The architecturally correct fix is at the producer, not the consumer: validate once in summarize.ts (F033's patch) and markdown.ts can legitimately trust `string[]`. Adding runtime array checks to every consumer of a validated type is the anti-pattern. (3) It is the third mirror of one defect — the producer is F033 (now medium) and the localStorage variant is F096 (medium); a test-file mirror should sit below both.
findings.reachability: No path of its own. markdown.ts only throws if a non-array `Summary` was already persisted, which requires F033's or F096's producer defect to fire first.
findings.blastRadius: One fixture in one 99-line test file; the consumer it under-tests (`bookToMarkdown`) has 2 call sites (itself via libraryToMarkdown, and the library export UI).
findings.amendedDescription: The `Summary` fixture at src/lib/markdown.test.ts:20-29 always supplies real arrays and the suite's only variation is the empty array at line 70, so `bookToMarkdown` is never exercised against a `Summary` whose array fields came off the wire — and markdown.ts:24-25 / :27-28 would throw `TypeError: ... .map is not a function` on a non-empty string. The observation is correct but low severity: the fixture is explicitly `Summary`-annotated and complete, the missing test could only be written with an `as unknown as Summary` cast that this audit flags as its own defect class, and the correct remedy is to validate once at the producer (F033, summarize.ts:36-37) rather than to add defensive array checks to every consumer of a type that is supposed to be validated. Third mirror of a defect already carried by F033 and F096.

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string compared numerically by isDue and lexically by repo.listDue, and nothing cross-checks them
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.dueAt` is typed `string` (`types.ts:92`) with the invariant "canonical ISO-8601 UTC timestamp" living only in comments. Two consumers read it with different orderings:
- `srs.ts:58` — `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()` (numeric, tolerant of any parseable format, yields `NaN` for garbage)
- `repo.ts:88` — `card.dueAt <= cutoff` (lexicographic string compare, correct only for zero-padded, same-offset ISO strings)

The `isDue` block in this file (lines 97-108) only ever feeds `dueAt` values it produced itself via `newCard`/`scheduleCard` or hand-wrote in canonical form. `repo.listDue` has no test at all (see L13-F13). So nothing anywhere pins the two comparisons to the same semantics. A non-padded `'2026-8-12'` is due under `isDue` and not due under `listDue`; `NaN` from an unparseable value makes `isDue` return `false` forever, so the card silently never surfaces again — a card that disappears rather than errors.

The type is the problem: `dueAt: string` lets any string in, and `ease`/`intervalDays` as bare `number`s are the same shape of footgun (`scheduleCard(card, grade)` is safe only because `Grade = 1|2|3|4` is a literal union — that part is done right). A branded `IsoTimestamp` produced by a single helper would make the two comparison sites provably consistent.

Verified sound in this file: `card(overrides)` on lines 7-22 builds from the real `newCard` factory and is annotated `: ReviewCard`, so the compiler enforces completeness — this is the honest-fixture pattern the rest of the suite should copy.
findings.verifierNote: The described test state is accurate: src/lib/srs.test.ts:97-109 is three `isDue` cases whose `dueAt` values are all canonical (`'2026-09-01T00:00:00.000Z'`, `NOW.toISOString()`, `'2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'`), and the fixture at :7-22 is annotated `: ReviewCard` and built from the real `newCard`, which is genuinely the honest-fixture pattern the finding praises. But this file contains no type weakness of its own: it is the test-side restatement of F092 (src/lib/srs.ts:33), filed under the same category with the same two comparison sites (srs.ts:58 numeric vs src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88 lexicographic) as its argument. Counting both at medium double-weights one structural observation. I also verified the coverage gap it leans on - `reviewCards.listDue` has zero tests, and src/lib/storage/repo.test.ts contains no occurrence of the string 'reviewCards' at all - but that is a coverage finding (and overlaps F098), not a type-safety medium.
findings.reachability: No runtime path. The file is a test; the behaviour it describes lives in srs.ts and repo.ts and is assessed under F092, where I found no producer of a non-canonical `dueAt`.
findings.blastRadius: 0 production call sites. The claim's real surface is `ReviewCard.dueAt` at src/types.ts:93 with 2 consumers (srs.ts:58, repo.ts:88-89), one of which has no production caller.
findings.suggestedPatch: Merge into F092 rather than fixing separately. If a test is wanted now, add the cheap cross-check to src/lib/srs.test.ts:97: assert that `isDue(card, now)` and `card.dueAt <= now.toISOString()` agree for the same fixture, which pins the two comparison semantics together. Risk: none - it is a new assertion over existing canonical fixtures.
findings.amendedDescription: Test-side restatement of F092. src/lib/srs.test.ts:97-109 exercises `isDue` only with canonical ISO `dueAt` values it produced itself, so nothing pins `isDue`'s numeric compare (srs.ts:58) to `reviewCards.listDue`'s lexicographic compare (repo.ts:88) - and `listDue` has no test at all. The file itself contains no `any`, assertion or suppression, and its `card()` fixture is annotated `: ReviewCard` and built from the real `newCard` factory, which is the correct pattern. Lowered to low and flagged for merge into F092 so one structural observation is not counted twice.

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string whose fixed-width-UTC-ISO invariant is unenforced, and two consumers compare it in incompatible ways
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.dueAt` is typed `string` (`src/types.ts:93`). Both producers in this file happen to write `Date.prototype.toISOString()` output (srs.ts:33 and srs.ts:52), but nothing in the type requires that, and two consumers depend on mutually incompatible readings of the same field:

- `src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88` filters with a LEXICOGRAPHIC compare: `owned.filter((card) => card.dueAt <= cutoff).sort((a, b) => a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt))`, with the comment 'ISO timestamps sort chronologically, so a string compare is enough'. That is only true for the fixed-width, `Z`-suffixed, 4-digit-year form.
- `src/lib/srs.ts:58` `isDue` uses a SEMANTIC compare: `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()`.

The two disagree on any other valid timestamp string, and `string` permits all of them. Concrete divergences: an offset form such as `'2026-08-12T10:00:00+02:00'` — a perfectly valid ISO 8601 string that many date libraries emit — parses correctly under `Date.parse` but sorts before every digit under a byte compare (`'+'` is 0x2B, `'2'` is 0x32), so `listDue` would report it due immediately and sort it first, forever. The extended-year form `toISOString()` itself emits for years outside 0000-9999 (`'+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z'`) has the same property. Separately, `Date.parse` on an unparseable string returns `NaN`, and `NaN <= x` is `false`, so `isDue` silently answers 'not due' — a card disappears from review permanently with no error, and the `boolean` return type hides that third state.

Compounding this: `isDue` has NO production caller. Grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/srs.test.ts`; the app uses the string compare in `repo.ts:88` exclusively. So the unit tests validate a due-date predicate the application never runs, while the predicate the application does run is untested against non-canonical input.

Correct behaviour: introduce a branded `IsoUtcTimestamp` (or `Millis`) constructed by one factory, so every producer is forced through the canonicalising path and the lexicographic-sort assumption in `repo.ts` becomes something the type actually guarantees. Then either delete `isDue` or make `repo.ts` use it, so there is one definition of 'due'.

Blast radius: `src/types.ts:93` (`dueAt`), plus every other bare-`string` timestamp field on the same types (`Book.addedAt`, `Book.finishedAt`, `Summary.generatedAt`, `Profile.createdAt`); producers at srs.ts:33,52; consumers at repo.ts:88-89 and srs.ts:58.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present and the two-comparisons observation is factually right: `ReviewCard.dueAt` is `string` at src/types.ts:93; producers are src/lib/srs.ts:33 and :52, both `toISOString()`; src/lib/srs.ts:58 compares with `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()` while src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 compares with `card.dueAt <= cutoff` then `localeCompare`. I confirmed the finding's strongest sub-claim by grep: `isDue` has ZERO production callers - src/lib/srs.test.ts is its only importer. But that cuts against the severity rather than for it. There is no path by which a non-canonical `dueAt` can enter the store: the only writer of `reviewCards` is `newCard` (srs.ts:22-36, called from src/components/QuizModal.tsx:52) and `scheduleCard` (srs.ts:42-55, called from src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38), both of which emit `toISOString()`; src/lib/storage/migrate.ts never touches `reviewCards`; and `LibraryExport` carries only books and summaries (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:94-98, :109-116), so the backup import cannot inject one either. No concrete call site exists where a wrong value arrives and compiles - the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. I also found the finding's headline mechanism inaccurate: it claims an offset form like '2026-08-12T10:00:00+02:00' 'sorts before every digit under a byte compare... so listDue would report it due immediately and sort it first, forever'. The '+' at index 19 only decides the comparison when the first 19 characters are identical; against a cutoff of '2026-08-12T09:00:00.000Z' the offset string compares GREATER at index 12 and is correctly not due. The unsoundness of mixing formats is real; that specific worked example is wrong.
findings.reachability: Not reachable today. Every `dueAt` in the store is `Date.prototype.toISOString()` output by construction, and no import, migration or external writer can produce another form. The `Date.parse` -> NaN -> permanently-not-due path exists only in `isDue`, which no production code calls.
findings.blastRadius: 1 field (src/types.ts:93) with 2 consumers, of which only src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 runs in production. Adopting a branded `IsoUtcTimestamp` properly would also touch `Book.addedAt`, `Book.finishedAt`, `Summary.generatedAt` and `Profile.createdAt` - a wide, mechanical retrofit with no live defect driving it.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest real win first: delete the dead `isDue` (src/lib/srs.ts:57-59) and its tests, or make repo.ts:88 call it, so there is exactly one definition of 'due'. If branding is wanted later: `export type IsoUtc = string & { readonly __iso: unique symbol }` with a single `toIsoUtc(d: Date): IsoUtc` factory, applied to `ReviewCard.dueAt` first. Risk: deleting `isDue` removes tested-but-unused API surface, so confirm no planned consumer before removing.
findings.amendedDescription: `ReviewCard.dueAt` is a bare `string` (src/types.ts:93) whose canonical-UTC-ISO invariant lives only in comments, and two consumers read it incompatibly: src/lib/srs.ts:58 semantically via `Date.parse`, src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88-89 lexicographically. Lowered to low because there is no reachable way for a non-canonical value to enter the store - `newCard` and `scheduleCard` are the only writers and both emit `toISOString()`, migrate.ts never writes `reviewCards`, and `LibraryExport` carries only books and summaries. The related real finding is that `isDue` has zero production callers (verified by grep), so the codebase tests a due-date predicate it never runs while the predicate it does run is untested; deleting `isDue` or routing repo.ts:88 through it is the concrete fix. Note also that the finding's worked example about a '+02:00' offset sorting first 'forever' is incorrect - the '+' only decides the byte compare when the preceding 19 characters match.

findings.title: scheduleCard declares a total return of ReviewCard but throws RangeError once ease/interval go non-finite; ease has a floor and no ceiling
findings.description:
`scheduleCard(card, grade, now): ReviewCard` cannot produce a `ReviewCard` for every input it accepts. Line 52 calls `new Date(now.getTime() + intervalDays * DAY_MS).toISOString()`, which throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` whenever the argument is `NaN` or outside the +/-8.64e15 ms Date range. Verified at runtime: `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` and `new Date(Infinity).toISOString()` both throw.

Two reachable triggers, both invisible to the compiler because `ease`, `intervalDays` and `reviewCount` are bare `number` on `ReviewCard` (`src/types.ts:91-94`):

1. Unbounded ease. `EASE_DELTA[4] = 0.1` and line 43 applies only a floor (`Math.max(MIN_EASE, ...)`) — there is no `MAX_EASE`. Ease therefore grows without limit, and line 46 multiplies the interval by `ease * 1.3` each time. Simulated: after 14 consecutive grade-4 ('Easy') reviews, `ease = 3.9` and `intervalDays = 480,395,074` (~1.3 million years), at which point `now + intervalDays * DAY_MS` exceeds the Date range and line 52 throws. Standard SM-2 caps ease; this implementation does not.
2. Non-finite input. `Math.max(1.3, NaN)` returns `NaN` and `Math.max(1, NaN)` returns `NaN` (both verified), so a single non-finite `card.ease` or `card.intervalDays` propagates straight through the floor guards into line 52. `ReviewCard` values are read back from IndexedDB via `getDb().getAll('reviewCards')` (`src/lib/storage/repo.ts:79,95`) where the `idb` DBSchema typing is a compile-time claim over rows with zero runtime validation.

Caller impact: `src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38` calls `await cardRepo.upsert(scheduleCard(current, gradeValue))` inside an async `useCallback` with no try/catch. A throw becomes an unhandled rejection: the grade button appears to do nothing, the card is never rescheduled, and the queue never advances — the review session dead-ends with no error surfaced.

Correct behaviour: cap ease (`MIN_EASE <= ease <= MAX_EASE`), clamp `intervalDays` to a sane maximum (e.g. 10 years), and express these as refined/branded numeric types constructed through one validating factory so the invariants are not re-implemented per call site. Alternatively make the return type honest about failure.

Blast radius: the single scheduling function behind the entire review feature; one call site (`useReviewQueue.ts:38`) but it is the only write path for review scheduling.
findings.verifierNote: The code defect is real and I reproduced it precisely. src/lib/srs.ts:43 applies only a floor (`Math.max(MIN_EASE, card.ease + EASE_DELTA[grade])`) with `EASE_DELTA[4] = 0.1` at :10 and no MAX_EASE anywhere in the file; :46 multiplies by `ease * INTERVAL_MODIFIER[grade]`; :52 calls `new Date(now.getTime() + intervalDays * DAY_MS).toISOString()`. What is wrong is the finding's assertion of 'two reachable triggers' - NEITHER is reachable. (1) Reaching review 14 requires 14 consecutive Easy grades on ONE card, and the queue is gated by `listDue` (repo.ts:84-90), which only returns cards whose `dueAt <= now`; the cumulative wall-clock wait across intervals 3, 11, 40, 151, 589, 2374, 9876, 42368, 187267, 852065, 3987664, 19180664, 94752480 days is roughly 325,000 years. `grade` also drops the card from the queue (`setQueue((rest) => rest.slice(1))`), so it cannot be re-graded within a session. (2) A non-finite `card.ease` has no producer: `reviewCards` is written only by `newCard` (ease 2.5) and `scheduleCard`, migrate.ts never touches the store, and the backup import carries only books and summaries. A latent, genuinely unreachable overflow is low, not medium.

findings.title: DBSchema value types promise every read row is a valid domain object, but IndexedDB validates nothing on the way out
findings.description: `BookSumDB` declares `books: { value: Book }`, `summaries: { value: Summary }` and so on, which makes `idb` type every read as `Book | undefined`, `Summary | undefined` etc. That is a guarantee IndexedDB structurally cannot provide: `db.get('books', id)` returns whatever object was structured-cloned in, by whatever code version wrote it, with zero shape checking. Today this is not merely theoretical — it is the read side of L02-F01. `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111` writes unvalidated objects from a user-supplied backup file into the `books` store, so the store genuinely can contain rows that are not `Book`s, and every subsequent `books.get` / `books.listByProfile` (`src/lib/storage/repo.ts:44,47`) hands them to callers stamped as valid. Note the compounding factor: `DB_VERSION` is 1 and the `upgrade` handler (db.ts:24-39) only ever runs the create-store path — it ignores the `oldVersion` argument `idb` supplies and contains no row-reshaping step, so there is no mechanism by which a malformed or older-shaped row would ever be repaired. The declared types are the app's only defence and they are compile-time only. Correct shape: keep the `DBSchema` value types as the intended shape, but treat `repo.ts` as the trust boundary — validate (or at least normalise required fields on) rows entering the store from any external source, so the type on the way out is earned rather than asserted.
findings.verifierNote: Everything factual in this finding checks out: src/lib/storage/db.ts:7-17 declares `books: { key: string; value: Book; ... }` etc., which makes `idb` type every read as `Book | undefined` with no runtime basis; `DB_VERSION` is 1 (db.ts:5) and the `upgrade(db)` handler at :24-39 ignores the `oldVersion` argument and only creates stores, so no row-reshaping path exists; and the real writer of unvalidated rows is present - src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111 `await bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })` over `payload.books` from a user-supplied backup, where the only guard upstream is `Array.isArray(data.books)` at src/components/ProfileView.tsx:119, which checks the array but never the shape of its elements. The problem is double-counting. This is the SCHEMA-SIDE statement of a defect already carried, at higher severity, by six other aggregate findings on the actual producer and consumer files: F004 (critical, ProfileView.tsx:117), F022 (high, useLibrary.tsx:102), F046 (high, repo.ts:8), F047 (high, repo.ts:44), F048 (high, repo.ts:52) and F049 (high, repo.ts:143). db.ts has no code to fix - the `DBSchema` value types are the correct declaration of intent, and the finding's own recommendation says so ('keep the DBSchema value types as the intended shape, but treat repo.ts as the trust boundary'), which is F046-F049's fix, not this one's. Keep it as the structural framing at low; the weight belongs on the producer findings.
findings.reachability: Reachable, but through the paths already counted: import a hand-edited or foreign backup JSON via ProfileView.tsx:109-135, and every subsequent `books.get`/`books.listByProfile` (repo.ts:44, :47) hands the malformed row out stamped as a `Book`. Nothing in db.ts can prevent or detect it.
findings.blastRadius: 5 store declarations in one file, 0 fixable lines. The consuming read paths are repo.ts:8, :13, :44, :47, :79, :95, :113, :143 - all already enumerated by F046-F049.
findings.suggestedPatch: No change in src/lib/storage/db.ts. Land the fix at the trust boundary instead, per F046-F049: add a `parseBook`/`parseSummary` normaliser in repo.ts applied on the write paths that accept external data (`books.create`, `summaries.upsert`) so the DBSchema type is earned. Risk: validating on the read path instead would cost a pass over every row on every list call - validate on write only.
findings.amendedDescription: src/lib/storage/db.ts:7-17 declares `DBSchema` value types (`value: Book`, `value: Summary`, ...) that make `idb` type every read as a valid domain object, a guarantee IndexedDB structurally cannot provide - and the store genuinely can hold non-conforming rows, because src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111 writes elements of a user-supplied backup file behind only an `Array.isArray` check (ProfileView.tsx:119). findings.title: blobs store key is a composite `${bookId}:${kind}` but is declared plain string, identical to the by-book index key
findings.description: The `blobs` store's primary key is not an id — it is a composite built by `src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126` (`const blobKey = (bookId: string, kind: BlobKind) => `${bookId}:${kind}``). The schema declares it as bare `string`, and the same store's `by-book` index key is also `string` but holds a raw `bookId`. Two structurally different key spaces are therefore the same type inside one store declaration, so `db.get('blobs', someBookId)` type-checks perfectly and simply returns `undefined` — a silent miss indistinguishable from 'no PDF stored', which in this app means the reader renders nothing rather than reporting an error. No current call site is wrong (repo.ts consistently routes through `blobKey`, and repo.ts:149-150 correctly feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results back to `delete`), so this is a latent footgun rather than a live bug — but it is a cheap one to close. Correct shape: `key: `${string}:${BlobKind}`` (a template-literal type, no runtime branding needed) — `blobKey()` already produces exactly that, so the only change is the declaration, and passing a bare bookId stops compiling. Two related observations from checking this store: `StoredBlob` (src/types.ts:67-80) also lets `key`, `bookId` and `kind` disagree with one another even though `repo.ts:133-139` always derives `key` from the other two; and every other declared index key type in this schema was verified correct against its `keyPath` (`by-profile` -> `profileId`, `by-book` -> `bookId`, `by-profile-due` -> `['profileId','dueAt']`), though `by-profile-due` is never actually queried since repo.ts:79 and :95 both do a full-store `getAll` and filter in memory.
findings.verifierNote: Factually correct on every point I checked. src/lib/storage/db.ts:11 declares `blobs: { key: string; value: StoredBlob; indexes: { 'by-book': string } }`, while the real primary key is composite - src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126 `const blobKey = (bookId: string, kind: BlobKind) => `${bookId}:${kind}``. Two different key spaces share one type inside one store declaration, so `db.get('blobs', someBookId)` compiles and silently returns `undefined`. src/types.ts:68-69 does document the format in a comment (`/** `${bookId}:${kind}` */ key: string;`) that the type does not encode. I verified the index declarations against their keyPaths in db.ts:28/31/34/38 and they are all correct, and that `by-profile-due` is indeed never queried (repo.ts:79 and :95 both do a full-store `getAll` and filter in memory). I also verified no call site is currently wrong: every blob access routes through `blobKey` (repo.ts:134, :143) and `removeByBook` at :147-151 feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results straight to `delete`. With no call site where a wrong value can arrive and compile, this is a structural recommendation, not a medium defect - which is exactly the bar this batch was told to apply to branded-type findings. The fix is genuinely cheap, so it belongs in the report as a low with a one-line patch rather than being dropped.

findings.title: The cascade test omits reviewCards, and the whole reviewCards store surface is untested
findings.description:
`removes the summary and blobs when a book is removed` asserts three things after `books.remove`: the book is gone, the summary is gone, the blob is gone. It does not assert that review cards are gone, even though `repo.ts:72` calls `reviewCards.removeByBook(id)` in that same cascade and `ReviewCard` rows carry a `bookId` foreign key. The profile-level cascade test on lines 88-97 has the same omission. Nothing in `repo.test.ts` touches `reviewCards` at all — `listByProfile`, `listDue`, `listByBook`, `upsert` and `removeByBook` (repo.ts:77-109) have zero coverage in the module's own suite.

That matters for type honesty because `reviewCards.listByProfile` and `listByBook` are raw `getDb().getAll('reviewCards')` reads typed solely by the `BookSumDB` schema declaration at `db.ts:12-16`. Nothing validates that a stored row is actually a `ReviewCard`; the declaration is an assertion about the contents of a store the app has been writing to since v1. Orphaned cards from a book deleted before the cascade existed would be returned as `ReviewCard[]` and fed to the review UI with a `bookId` that resolves to nothing.

More generally, every read test in this file is a closed loop: the suite writes with `profiles.create`/`books.create`, then reads back with `profiles.list`/`books.listByProfile`. No fixture ever puts a record into the store that the repo did not itself construct, so the schema's type claims can never be falsified. `profiles.list` at `repo.ts:9` does `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` — an unguarded dereference on a field that only the repo's own writer guarantees.

Grepping repo.test.ts for 'reviewCards' returns zero hits, so `listByProfile`, `listDue`, `listByBook`, `upsert` and `removeByBook` (repo.ts:77-109) have no coverage in the module's own suite. The observation that every read test is a closed loop - fixtures only ever enter via the repo's own writers, so the DBSchema type claims can never be falsified - is also true and is a good one. But this is a test-coverage finding wearing a `boundary-without-validation` category: the type-safety half of the argument ('`listByProfile`/`listByBook` are raw `getAll('reviewCards')` reads typed solely by the db.ts declaration') is F094, which I have in turn amended down as the schema-side mirror of F046-F049. findings.title: profiles.update and books.update write whatever the caller hands them, persisting NaN as a typed number
findings.description: Both update methods are a straight pass-through to put() with no validation - the record's correctness rests entirely on the caller's static type. That is not sufficient because a value can satisfy `number` and still be garbage: src/components/ProfileView.tsx:239 sets `monthlyGoal: parseInt(e.target.value)`, and parseInt('') is NaN, which is a `number` as far as the compiler is concerned. Clearing the monthly-goal field and saving persists `Profile.monthlyGoal = NaN` through repo.ts:31. ProfileView.tsx:53 then computes `Math.min(100, (finishedCount / NaN) * 100)` = NaN and renders a NaN-width progress bar. The corruption also outlives the session: structured clone preserves NaN in IndexedDB, and JSON.stringify in the backup export turns it into null, so a subsequent import writes `monthlyGoal: null` under a `number` declaration. Blast radius: 26 profiles.* and 22 books.* call sites read records these two methods can poison. Correct behaviour: the repo's write boundary should reject non-finite numbers and empty required strings rather than trusting the declared type.
findings.verifierNote: The finding's sole named failure mode is FALSE. I opened src/components/ProfileView.tsx around line 239 and the control is `<input type="range" min="1" max="20" value={editedProfile.monthlyGoal} onChange={(e) => setEditedProfile({ ...editedProfile, monthlyGoal: parseInt(e.target.value) })} />`. A range input has no empty state - the browser guarantees `.value` is always a valid numeric string and clamps it into [min,max] - so 'clearing the monthly-goal field and saving' is not an action the UI offers and `parseInt` can never return NaN there. I swept every other numeric coercion in src/components, src/features and src/app: only AddBookModal.tsx:162 `setRating(Number(e.target.value))` (an `<input type="number">`, where an emptied field yields `''` and `Number('') === 0`, not NaN) and AudioPlayer.tsx:69/:87 (transient playback state, never persisted). There is no producer of a non-finite number on any persisted path. What remains true is only that src/lib/storage/repo.ts:30-33 and :63-66 are unvalidated pass-throughs to `put()` - which is a design property of a thin repo, and is already counted at high by F048 (repo.ts:52, 'books.create and summaries.upsert persist caller objects with no validation') and F046/F047 on the read side. The blast radius was also inflated: I measured 9 non-test `profiles.*` call sites and 14 non-test `books.*` call sites, not the claimed 26 and 22.
findings.reachability: The claimed path is not reachable: a range slider cannot be cleared. The residual - a caller handing `update()` a structurally valid but semantically wrong record - is reachable only through the backup-import path already covered by F004 (critical) and F022 (high), and that path goes through `books.create`, not `update`.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 9 `profiles.*` and 14 `books.*` non-test call sites (the finding claimed 26 and 22 - inflated roughly 2x, consistent with this audit's known test-file overcount). Two update methods, both thin.
findings.amendedDescription: src/lib/storage/repo.ts:30-33 (`profiles.update`) and :63-66 (`books.update`) are unvalidated pass-throughs to `put()`, so record correctness rests entirely on the caller's static type. REFUTED sub-claim: the finding's only concrete failure - that src/components/ProfileView.tsx:239 persists `monthlyGoal: NaN` when the user clears the field - cannot happen. That control is `<input type="range" min="1" max="20">`, which has no empty state and always yields a valid numeric string, so `parseInt` never returns NaN. No other persisted path produces a non-finite number either (AddBookModal.tsx:162 uses `Number()` on a number input, and `Number('')` is 0). Lowered to low - the residual observation is real but duplicates F048 (high, repo.ts:52) on the write side and F046/F047 on the read side.

findings.title: Every identifier in the persistence API is a bare string, including two adjacent methods that take different id kinds
findings.description: profileId, bookId, summaryId and blobKey are all `string`, so the compiler cannot tell them apart anywhere in the repo's public surface. The sharpest foot-gun is inside `summaries`: getByBook(bookId) at line 112 and remove(id) at line 121 are seven lines apart and take different kinds of id with identical types. books.remove at 68-73 gets it right (`summaries.getByBook(id)` then `summaries.remove(summary.id)`), but `summaries.remove(id)` with the book id compiles cleanly and silently deletes nothing - an orphaned summary that later collides with a regenerated one. Same exposure for blobKey(bookId, kind) at line 126 (a summaryId compiles and produces a key that will never match), reviewCards.removeByBook(bookId) vs the card ids deleted at line 107, and books.create's input where profileId and the optional id are both string. Related: StoredBlob.key is documented as `${bookId}:${kind}` (types.ts:68) but declared `string`, where a template-literal type would enforce the format blobKey produces. Blast radius: every exported repo method except blobs.put takes at least one bare-string id - 75+ call sites across src pass ids positionally. Correct behaviour: branded id types (BookId, ProfileId, SummaryId) minted at creation, which is a moderate but mechanical retrofit since all ids originate from newId() at line 4.

But I checked every call site and none is wrong: repo.ts:70 correctly does `summaries.getByBook(id)` then `summaries.remove(summary.id)`; :106-107 deletes by `card.id` after `listByBook(bookId)`; :149-150 feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results straight to `delete`; and outside repo.ts, `summaryRepo.getByBook` is only ever passed a book id (useLibrary.tsx:76, :92) and `summaryRepo.upsert` a full `Summary` (useLibrary.tsx:48, :80, :115, migrate.ts:122).
