findings.title: setup.ts provides no typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs diverge from typeof fetch and one leaks across tests
findings.description:
`setup.ts` wires jest-dom, fake-indexeddb, an `asyncUtilTimeout` and an `afterEach` cleanup — but no shared browser-API stubbing. Every suite that needs `fetch` hand-rolls its own, and `vi.stubGlobal(name, value: unknown)` accepts anything, so the compiler never checks any of them against `typeof globalThis.fetch`. Four divergent stubs result:
- `smoke.test.tsx:43` — `(input: RequestInfo | URL) => Promise<Response>`, drops the `init` parameter entirely
- `covers/index.test.ts:8` — same, drops `init`
- `covers/index.test.ts:56` — `async () => { throw ... }`, zero parameters, inferred `Promise<never>`
- `covers/index.test.ts:64` — drops `init` again
Dropping `init` means any production `fetch(url, { signal, headers, method })` has its options silently discarded under test, and any assertion written over `call[1]` would be untypeable. Real `fetch` returns `Promise<Response>` and can reject; the `Promise<never>` stub is not assignable to it and nothing says so.

Second, concrete consequence of there being no shared helper: `smoke.test.tsx:61` calls `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` as the last statement of the test BODY rather than in an `afterEach`. `restoreMocks: true` in `vite.config.ts:24` restores spies but does not undo `stubGlobal`, and `unstubGlobals` is not set. If any assertion between lines 49 and 60 fails, the stubbed `fetch` — which answers every request with a fixed 200 `{}` — leaks into the two later tests in the same file, silently changing what they exercise. `covers/index.test.ts:16-18` gets this right with an `afterEach`; nothing enforces the difference.

The fix shape is a single typed helper in `setup.ts` (`stubFetch(fn: typeof globalThis.fetch)`) plus `unstubGlobals: true`, which restores the compiler check and centralises teardown. Also absent: any stub for `URL.createObjectURL`/`revokeObjectURL` (see L13-F10).
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present. src/test/setup.ts is 14 lines (jest-dom, fake-indexeddb, configure({asyncUtilTimeout:5000}) at line 9, afterEach cleanup at 11-14) with no fetch helper. All four stubs verified: smoke.test.tsx:43, covers/index.test.ts:8, :56 (zero-param throwing stub), :64. vite.config.ts:24 sets restoreMocks:true with no unstubGlobals, and smoke.test.tsx:61 does call vi.unstubAllGlobals() as the last statement of the test BODY while covers/index.test.ts:16-18 uses afterEach — the asymmetry is real. Two claims overstate: (a) a one-parameter function IS legally assignable to typeof fetch in TS, so 'drops init' is not a type error and no production init is 'silently discarded' any differently than by a stub that ignores it; (b) the category unknown-misuse points at vitest's own vi.stubGlobal(name, value: unknown) signature, which is third-party, not source — the spec excludes library-side types from per-file findings. What survives is genuine but test-only: nothing checks the stubs against typeof globalThis.fetch, and the leak risk at smoke.test.tsx:61 is real test hygiene rather than a type weakness. Spec reserves low for exactly this ('any in test fixtures ... worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents').
findings.reachability: Test-only. If any assertion between smoke.test.tsx:49-60 throws, line 61 never runs and the 200-'{}' stub leaks into the two later tests in the file (lines 64 and 85), which would then exercise a stubbed network. No production path is affected.
findings.blastRadius: 4 stub sites in 2 test files; 0 production files.
findings.suggestedPatch: In src/test/setup.ts add `export function stubFetch(impl: typeof globalThis.fetch) { vi.stubGlobal('fetch', vi.fn(impl)); }` and extend the existing afterEach (line 11) with `vi.unstubAllGlobals();`. Replace the four hand-rolled stubs with stubFetch(...) and delete smoke.test.tsx:61 plus covers/index.test.ts:16-18. Risk: the global unstub in afterEach would also clear a stub a test intended to outlive it — no test does that today.
findings.amendedDescription: src/test/setup.ts provides no shared, typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs (smoke.test.tsx:43; covers/index.test.ts:8, :56, :64) are each written against an ad-hoc signature that nothing checks against `typeof globalThis.fetch`. The practical consequence is not the omitted `init` parameter (legal in TS) but that `mock.calls` entries are typed to whatever the stub declared, so an assertion over the request options is untypeable, and that cleanup is per-file convention: smoke.test.tsx:61 unstubs inside the test body, so a failing assertion at lines 49-60 leaks a blanket 200 stub into the rest of the file. Test-hygiene severity; no production path is affected.

findings.title: The 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant is asserted by a for-loop that runs zero times when nothing is captured
findings.description:
`makes no network call to Gemini on boot` guards one of CLAUDE.md's stated invariants, and its entire assertion is a `for` loop over `fetchSpy.mock.calls`. If `mock.calls` is empty the loop body never executes and the test passes having asserted nothing at all. There is no `expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalled()`, no `expect.assertions(n)`, and no check that the spy was actually installed in the path under test.

That makes the test indistinguishable between three outcomes: (a) boot genuinely made no request — the intended pass; (b) boot made requests through a `fetch` reference captured at module-import time, before `vi.stubGlobal` ran on line 47, so the spy never saw them; (c) a future refactor moves the network call somewhere the spy does not cover. Only (a) is the invariant; all three are green.

The stub also returns a fixed `new Response('{}', { status: 200 })` for every URL, so even if a Gemini call happened it would be answered successfully rather than surfacing as a failure. The identical pattern is at `covers/index.test.ts:72-74` (`never calls a Gemini endpoint`), where the loop does currently run — but nothing keeps it that way.

What goes untested: whether the spy is on the path at all. The cheap fix is asserting a non-zero call count (or `expect.hasAssertions()`) alongside the URL check.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present exactly as described: smoke.test.tsx:58-60 is `for (const call of fetchSpy.mock.calls) { expect(String(call[0])).not.toContain('generativelanguage'); }` with no expect.assertions and no toHaveBeenCalled, so on the intended-pass path (zero captured calls) the assertion body never executes. That is a genuinely vacuous test guarding a stated CLAUDE.md invariant. However this is a test-assertion-strength defect, not a type weakness: nothing here is typed via assertion and no external data enters typed code, so the assigned category boundary-without-validation does not hold. The only type-adjacent residue is that the stub at line 43 declares one parameter, so `call` is a 1-tuple and `String(call[0])` is the only expressible assertion (see F101). Discovery's alternative (b) — a fetch reference captured at module-import time before the stub at line 47 — is not supported: the Gemini client is resolved lazily via getClient() at call time, not at import.
findings.reachability: The vacuous branch is the normal green path — the test passes today having asserted nothing. A future refactor that moves the Gemini call outside the spy's reach would also pass silently.
findings.blastRadius: 1 test; the same vacuous-loop shape is repeated at covers/index.test.ts:72-74.
findings.suggestedPatch: Replace smoke.test.tsx:58-60 with `const geminiCalls = fetchSpy.mock.calls.filter(([input]) => String(input).includes('generativelanguage')); expect(geminiCalls).toEqual([]);` and move vi.unstubAllGlobals() out of the body into an afterEach. Risk: none — the new form fails on exactly the same condition but is non-vacuous and prints the offending URL.
findings.amendedDescription: smoke.test.tsx:58-60 asserts the 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant with a for-loop over fetchSpy.mock.calls that runs zero times on the intended-pass path, so the test passes having asserted nothing. Real test-strength defect (the invariant is unguarded against a refactor that moves the call outside the spy), but it is not a type-safety finding: no external data is typed by assertion here. Reclassified low.

findings.title: Book/Summary/Profile/ReviewCard ids are all bare string, and one adjacent-line call site would silently swallow a swap
findings.description: Every entity id in the domain model is `string`: `Book.id`/`Book.profileId`/`Book.summaryId`, `Summary.id`/`Summary.bookId`, `Profile.id`, `ReviewCard.id`/`profileId`/`bookId`. The repo signatures are correspondingly indistinguishable — `books.get(id: string)`, `books.remove(id: string)`, `summaries.remove(id: string)` (a summary id) and `profiles.get(id: string)` all accept any of them. The concrete swap-compiles site is `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:81-83`, where three different id kinds are juggled across three adjacent lines: `const book = await bookRepo.get(summary.bookId); if (book && book.summaryId !== summary.id) await bookRepo.update({ ...book, summaryId: summary.id })`. Writing `bookRepo.get(summary.id)` instead of `bookRepo.get(summary.bookId)` type-checks, returns `undefined`, and the very next line's `if (book && ...)` guard swallows it — the summary/book link is silently never written, with no throw and no log, and the book keeps rendering as unsummarised. `reviewCards.listByProfile(profileId: string)` and `reviewCards.listByBook(bookId: string)` (repo.ts:78, 94) likewise have identical signatures and different meanings. Correct shape: branded aliases (`type BookId = string & { readonly __brand: 'BookId' }`, etc.) applied at the `types.ts` declarations and threaded through the repo signatures; per the audit spec this is a retrofit cost, so prioritise `BookId` vs `SummaryId` (the pair with a demonstrated silent-failure path) over the rest.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present: types.ts:29-30 (Book.id, profileId), :50 (summaryId), :55-56 (Summary.id, bookId), :18 (Profile.id), :84-86 (ReviewCard ids) are all bare `string`, and repo.ts:12/47/68/112/121 accept an undifferentiated `id: string`, so any id kind satisfies any signature. The cited call site is real and reads exactly as quoted at useLibrary.tsx:81-83. But it is a hypothetical-typo hazard, not a wrong value arriving: no producer in the codebase passes the wrong id kind, and per the established baseline the backfill at useLibrary.tsx:82-83 is dead code (addBook at lines 44-45 always sets summaryId when a summary exists, so `book.summaryId !== summary.id` is never true on the live path). The spec's own note applies — branded types are 'easy to recommend, hard to retrofit' — and the bar of a concrete call site where a wrong value could actually arrive and compile is not met. Downgrading to low, which is where the spec puts hygiene-grade type weakness.
findings.reachability: No live path. The failure requires a future edit to substitute one id for another; the immediate `if (book && ...)` guard at useLibrary.tsx:82 would then swallow the resulting undefined silently.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted non-test id-accepting call sites: books 12 (useLibrary 32/45/62/70/81/83/91/106/111/136/150, migrate 105), summaries 6 (useLibrary 48/76/80/92/115, migrate 122), reviewCards 4 (QuizModal 49/52, useReviewQueue 20/38), blobs 4 (BookDetail 197, useLibrary 51, migrate 137/143). Only one site — useLibrary.tsx:81 — juggles two id kinds in one expression.
findings.suggestedPatch: If taken: `type Brand<K, T> = K & { readonly __brand: T }; export type BookId = Brand<string, 'BookId'>; export type SummaryId = Brand<string, 'SummaryId'>;` in types.ts, with casts confined to the three producers (repo.ts:4 newId, the route param at useBookRoute.ts:8, and the import path at useLibrary.tsx:109-115). Risk: every test fixture and every string-literal id in the suite needs a cast, so the change is wide even though it is mechanical — treat as a structural recommendation, not a fix.
findings.amendedDescription: All entity ids are bare `string`, so repo signatures (repo.ts:12/47/68/112/121) cannot distinguish a book id from a summary id and a swap would compile. The nearest juggling site, useLibrary.tsx:81-83, is dead code on the live path, and no producer currently passes the wrong kind — this is a latent refactor hazard rather than a present defect.

findings.title: Book.category is an unconstrained string fed by the LLM, while the Category enum declared right above it is dead code
findings.description: `types.ts:6-15` exports a `Category` enum with eight members, and `types.ts:33` then declares `Book.category` as bare `string`. A search across `src/` finds no reference to the `Category` identifier anywhere outside its own declaration — the only other hits are unrelated JSX label text and `activeCategory` locals — so the enum is dead and the field it was written for is unconstrained. Producers write free-form strings: `'Other'` at `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:154`, `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:109` and `src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:26`, and otherwise whatever Gemini returns, since `src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:8` declares `category: { type: Type.STRING }` with no enum constraint and `RawBookResponse.category?: string` is asserted straight out of `JSON.parse` at summarize.ts:52. Consumers then compare that string exactly: `src/features/library/LibraryPage.tsx:47` filters with `book.category === activeCategory`, and `src/components/StatsView.tsx:23-28` builds the entire Category Breakdown chart by grouping on the raw string. Concrete failure: the model returns 'Self-Help' for one book and 'self-help' for another; the stats chart shows them as two separate categories with a count of 1 each, and the library filter chip for one will never match the other. Correct behaviour: type `Book.category` as the `Category` enum (or a string-literal union) and normalise the AI-supplied value against that set at the `summarize.ts` boundary, falling back to `Other` — the enum to do it with already exists.
findings.verifierNote: Both halves of the pattern verified. types.ts:6-15 declares the eight-member `Category` enum and types.ts:33 declares `category: string`; a repo-wide grep for the identifier returns only its own declaration at types.ts:6 — every other hit is JSX label text (BookDetail.tsx:321, StatsView.tsx:133/138) or an `activeCategory` local (LibraryPage.tsx:22/47/110/174-177). The enum is dead. Producers confirmed: summarize.ts:26 `category: data.category || 'Other'` where data is the raw JSON.parse cast at summarize.ts:52/73, schemas.ts:8 `category: { type: Type.STRING }` with no enum constraint, useLibrary.tsx:154 and migrate.ts:109. What breaks Discovery's severity is the consumer: LibraryPage.tsx:65 builds the chip list as `['All', ...Array.from(new Set(books.map((b) => b.category)))]` — derived from the books themselves — so the exact-match filter at LibraryPage.tsx:47 always has a matching chip and no book is ever unreachable. The real consequence is fragmentation ('Self-Help' vs 'Self Help' become two chips and two rows in the StatsView breakdown at StatsView.tsx:23-28), which is cosmetic. Spec low: 'worth fixing for hygiene but won't cause incidents'.
findings.reachability: Every AI-generated book takes an arbitrary Gemini string into Book.category and into IndexedDB. It renders and filters correctly; it merely fragments the filter chips and the category breakdown.
findings.blastRadius: One dead enum; four producers (summarize.ts:26, useLibrary.tsx:154, migrate.ts:109, plus the raw model value); three consumers (LibraryPage.tsx:47/65, StatsView.tsx:23-28, markdown.ts:13).
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheapest honest fix: delete the dead enum at types.ts:6-15. If the constraint is wanted instead, add `enum: Object.values(Category)` to schemas.ts:8 and coerce at summarize.ts:26 (`category: (Object.values(Category) as string[]).includes(data.category ?? '') ? data.category! : 'Other'`), leaving Book.category as `string` so already-stored free-form values still load. Risk: narrowing Book.category to the enum type would make existing IndexedDB rows violate their declared type — do not do that without a migration.
findings.amendedDescription: types.ts:6-15 exports a `Category` enum that no code references, while types.ts:33 leaves Book.category an unconstrained string filled by Gemini (schemas.ts:8 has no enum constraint; summarize.ts:26 takes the value straight off the JSON.parse cast). Consumers compare exactly (LibraryPage.tsx:47) but the chip list at LibraryPage.tsx:65 is derived from the stored books, so no book becomes unreachable — the consequence is category fragmentation in the filter chips and the StatsView breakdown, plus a dead enum that misleads readers.

findings.title: The quiz-question shape is declared three separate times across types.ts and srs.ts
findings.description: `QuizQuestion` (types.ts:105-110) declares `question`, `options`, `correctAnswerIndex`, `explanation`. `ReviewCard` (types.ts:86-89) re-declares the identical four fields inline alongside its id and SRS fields. `NewCardInput` (src/lib/srs.ts:13-20) declares them a third time alongside `profileId`/`bookId`, and `src/lib/srs.ts:26-30` then copies them across field-by-field. One shape, three declarations, one hand-written copy loop. Adding or renaming a quiz field means editing three types and the copy loop, and the compiler only flags a subset of those — a field added to `QuizQuestion` alone silently fails to reach `ReviewCard`, which is how quiz data would quietly stop being persisted. Correct shape: define the four fields once and compose — `interface ReviewCard extends QuizQuestion { id; profileId; bookId; ease; intervalDays; dueAt; reviewCount }` and `type NewCardInput = QuizQuestion & { profileId: string; bookId: string }` — which also collapses the copy loop in `newCard` to a spread.
findings.verifierNote: Three declarations verified line by line: `QuizQuestion` at types.ts:105-110 (`question`, `options`, `correctAnswerIndex`, `explanation`); the same four inline on `ReviewCard` at types.ts:87-90; and again on `NewCardInput` at srs.ts:13-20 - plus the hand-written field-by-field copy at srs.ts:27-30 inside `newCard`. The failure mode claimed is real and mechanical: a field added to `QuizQuestion` alone reaches neither `ReviewCard` nor the copy loop, and nothing errors, so newly-generated quiz data would silently fail to persist. This is exactly the spec's `generic-opportunity` definition ('duplicated type definitions across modules that could collapse'), and unlike the other two generic-opportunity findings in this batch there really are duplicated declarations here. Not generated code.
findings.reachability: The copy loop at srs.ts:22-36 runs for every quiz question turned into a review card - the whole spaced-repetition feature.
findings.blastRadius: 3 type declarations across 2 files plus 1 copy loop; `ReviewCard` is the IndexedDB record shape (db.ts, repo.reviewCards) so the composition must be behaviour-preserving.
findings.suggestedPatch: `export interface ReviewCard extends QuizQuestion { id: string; profileId: string; bookId: string; ease: number; intervalDays: number; dueAt: string; reviewCount: number; }` (move `QuizQuestion` above it in types.ts), `export type NewCardInput = QuizQuestion & { profileId: string; bookId: string };`, and collapse srs.ts:23-35 to `{ ...input, id: crypto.randomUUID(), ease: STARTING_EASE, intervalDays: 1, dueAt: now.toISOString(), reviewCount: 0 }`. Risk: the spread version copies any extra property present on `input` at runtime, so keep `NewCardInput` exact-shaped; the persisted record shape is unchanged.

findings.title: noImplicitOverride is off — one unmarked override in the AI error class hierarchy
findings.description:
`noImplicitOverride` is not enabled. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride` produces exactly 1 error, at `src/lib/ai/errors.ts:15`, where a constructor parameter property redeclares a member inherited from `Error` without an `override` modifier.

Without the flag, a subclass member that shadows a base-class member is indistinguishable from one that was meant to be new. On an `Error` subclass this is the classic footgun: silently redeclaring `message`, `name` or `cause` as a parameter property can shadow the base field that `Error.prototype.toString`, the `stack` header and most logging paths read from, so the error renders with an empty or stale message while the subclass field holds the real one. It also means a future rename in the base type would silently orphan the subclass member rather than erroring.

Correct behaviour: enable `noImplicitOverride` and add the explicit `override` keyword at that one site — or, if the redeclaration is not actually intended to override, drop the parameter property and pass the value through to `super()`. Adoption cost: trivial, one line, and it is the only blocker for turning the flag on permanently.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json
  8      "strict": true,          // noImplicitOverride is NOT part of the strict family

$ npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride   (1 error; baseline 0)
  src/lib/ai/errors.ts(15,5): error TS4115: This parameter property must have an
    'override' modifier because it overrides a member in base class 'Error'.
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured myself: `npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride` produces exactly one error - `src/lib/ai/errors.ts(15,5): error TS4115: This parameter property must have an 'override' modifier because it overrides a member in base class 'Error'.` - against a baseline of 0. Confirmed at the source: errors.ts:15 declares `readonly cause?: unknown` as a constructor parameter property while `Error.cause` already exists in the ES2022 lib the project targets (tsconfig.json:3-4), so the subclass field genuinely shadows a base member. tsconfig.json:8 has `strict: true` and `noImplicitOverride` is correctly identified as outside the strict family. The general risk described (silently redeclaring `message`/`name`/`cause` and desynchronising from what `Error.prototype.toString` and the `stack` header read) is the right rationale; here it is benign because the parameter property assigns the same value `super()` would have. Adoption cost is one line.
findings.reachability: `AiError` is constructed on every AI failure (errors.ts:63) and `cause` is written every time. No current misbehaviour - the shadowing is value-identical.
findings.blastRadius: 1 site; enabling the flag is a whole-project ratchet with exactly this one blocker.
findings.suggestedPatch: Preferred: stop shadowing - drop the parameter property and pass the value through, `constructor(readonly kind: AiErrorKind, message: string, cause?: unknown) { super(message, { cause }); this.name = 'AiError'; }`, then add `"noImplicitOverride": true` to tsconfig.json. Risk: `super(message, { cause })` sets `cause` only when the ES2022 Error options overload is present (it is, given `target`/`lib` ES2022), and it makes `cause` non-enumerable where the parameter property made it enumerable - if any code enumerates AiError's own keys, use `override readonly cause?: unknown` instead.

findings.title: Four zero-cost strictness flags are unset — they add 0 errors today but nothing locks the property in
findings.description:
Four checking flags outside the `strict` family are not enabled, and each measures **0 errors** against the current source, so enabling them is a pure ratchet with no remediation work at all:

- `noImplicitReturns` (0 errors) — would catch a function with a conditional return path that falls through to `undefined`.
- `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` (0 errors) — would catch `import './missing.css'`-style imports that resolve to nothing.
- `allowUnreachableCode: false` (0 errors) — currently unreachable code is a suggestion-level hint, not an error.
- `allowUnusedLabels: false` (0 errors).

Because `strict: true` already covers the whole strict family (verified below), these four plus the flags in L01-F02/F03/F05/F09 are the entire remaining strictness surface. The codebase is clean enough today that all four can be turned on in a single commit with no code changes; leaving them off means the first violation lands silently rather than failing CI.

For completeness, I verified that `strict: true` really does enable every sub-flag in TypeScript 6.0.3 — passing each explicitly adds 0 errors: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitThis`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. So there is no hidden strict-family gap; the codebase is genuinely null-aware, and the multi-week `strictNullChecks` migration the audit spec warns about does not apply here.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json — current checking flags
  8      "strict": true,
  9      "noUnusedLocals": true,
 10      "noUnusedParameters": true,
 11      "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
 12      "isolatedModules": true,

$ npx tsc --noEmit --<flag>        (error counts, baseline 0)
  noImplicitReturns              0      strictNullChecks             0
  noUncheckedSideEffectImports   0      strictFunctionTypes          0
  allowUnreachableCode false     0      strictBindCallApply          0
  allowUnusedLabels false        0      strictPropertyInitialization 0
  noImplicitAny                  0      strictBuiltinIteratorReturn  0
  noImplicitThis                 0      useUnknownInCatchVariables   0
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured all four flags against the current tree, each on top of the existing config: `--noImplicitReturns`, `--noUncheckedSideEffectImports`, `--allowUnreachableCode false` and `--allowUnusedLabels false` each produce 0 errors, matching the finding exactly. tsconfig.json:8-12 confirms the current checking flags (`strict`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `isolatedModules`) and none of the four is present. This is a genuine `tsconfig-strictness-gap` with zero remediation cost - the honest 'be honest about the cost of strictness flags' caveat in the spec cuts in this finding's favour rather than against it. `low` is the right tier: nothing is broken, the value is a ratchet that makes the first violation fail CI instead of landing silently.
findings.reachability: n/a - a configuration gap, not a code path. No current source violates any of the four.
findings.blastRadius: Whole program (tsconfig.json applies to all 86 files in `include`), but zero files need changing.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add to tsconfig.json compilerOptions alongside :9-11: `"noImplicitReturns": true, "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true, "allowUnreachableCode": false, "allowUnusedLabels": false`. Risk: none measured today; `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` is the only one that can start failing on a dependency bump (a package whose side-effect-only import stops resolving), so land it in its own commit if CI stability matters.

findings.title: skipLibCheck: true masks an unresolved module in the @google/genai type surface (legitimate, but undocumented)
findings.description:
`skipLibCheck: true` is set. Measured what it hides: `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` produces exactly 2 errors, both in `node_modules`, none in source:

1. `node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29)` — cannot resolve `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`. This is an **optional** peer dependency of `@google/genai` (`peerDependenciesMeta: { "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": { optional: true } }`) and is deliberately not installed.
2. `node_modules/@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23)` — cannot find type definitions for `jest`, which this project correctly does not have (it uses Vitest).

So `skipLibCheck` is load-bearing, not laziness — this is the "compatibility lock-in" pattern the audit spec says to isolate rather than rip out, and the recommendation is NOT to turn it off. Blast radius today is nil: the unresolved `Client` type is only referenced by `@google/genai`'s MCP tool helper, and the app imports only `GoogleGenAI`, `Chat`, `Type` and `Modality` (`src/lib/ai/client.ts:1`, `chat.ts:1`, `schemas.ts:1`, `tts.ts:1`), none of which touch it.

The real gap is that this is undocumented. Every other non-obvious setting in this repo carries a comment explaining why (see `vite.config.ts:5-8` and `:13-15`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:15-16`), but `skipLibCheck` does not — so a future contributor cannot tell whether it is deliberate insulation or an unexamined default, and will not know that flipping it breaks the build for a reason unrelated to their change. Correct behaviour: add a comment naming both causes, and re-run `--skipLibCheck false` on dependency bumps so newly-introduced third-party type drift is noticed rather than permanently silenced.
findings.evidence:
tsconfig.json
 14      "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
 15      "skipLibCheck": true,          // <-- no comment explaining what it is insulating
 16      "noEmit": true,

$ npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false   (2 errors, both third-party)
  node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29): error TS2307:
    Cannot find module '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js'
  node_modules/@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23): error TS2688:
    Cannot find type definition file for 'jest'

@google/genai package.json: peerDependenciesMeta.@modelcontextprotocol/sdk.optional === true
findings.verifierNote: Re-measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` produces exactly the 2 errors claimed, both under node_modules and none in source - `@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29) TS2307` for the unresolved `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`, and `@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23) TS2688` for the absent `jest` types (this project uses Vitest). tsconfig.json:15 confirms `"skipLibCheck": true` with no adjacent comment, while other non-obvious settings in the repo are commented. This is precisely the spec's 'compatibility lock-in' pattern and the finding correctly does NOT recommend turning it off; the audit-author note that a suppression-with-a-reason is still a finding whose recommendation is documentation-and-isolation is what keeps it in scope. `low` is correct.
findings.reachability: n/a - both suppressed errors are in third-party declaration files. The unresolved MCP `Client` type is only referenced by @google/genai's tool helper, which this app never imports.
findings.blastRadius: Whole program, but zero source files are affected; the only cost is a future contributor's inability to tell deliberate insulation from an unexamined default.
findings.suggestedPatch: Keep the flag; add a comment at tsconfig.json:15, e.g. `// Two third-party declaration files fail --skipLibCheck false: @google/genai references the optional @modelcontextprotocol/sdk peer (deliberately not installed) and @testing-library/jest-dom references jest types (this project uses Vitest). Re-run `tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` after dependency bumps.` Risk: `format:check` runs `prettier --check .` over tsconfig.json, so confirm Prettier preserves the JSONC comment before committing.

findings.title: Vitest and jest-dom globals are in the type scope of production source, not just tests
findings.description:
`"types": ["vite/client", "vitest/globals", "@testing-library/jest-dom"]` applies to the whole program, and `node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts` uses `declare global` to publish `describe`, `it`, `test`, `expect`, `vi`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` and friends. Combined with `include: ["src", "vite.config.ts"]` — a single program covering all 86 source files, of which 21 are tests — this means a production module such as `src/lib/storage/repo.ts` or a React component can reference `vi.fn()` or `expect(...)` and `tsc --noEmit` will accept it. The failure only appears in the browser at runtime as `vi is not defined`, and it ships in the bundle.

ESLint does not backstop this either: `no-undef` is explicitly disabled for TypeScript files by the `tseslint` recommended preset (confirmed via `--print-config`: `no-undef: [0, {"typeof": false}]`), on the assumption that the compiler catches undefined identifiers — which here it does not, because the globals are genuinely declared.

Correct behaviour: split the program so test globals are scoped to test files — either a `tsconfig.test.json` covering `**/*.test.ts(x)` and `src/test/**` that adds `vitest/globals` and `@testing-library/jest-dom`, with the root config dropping them; or drop `globals: true` from `vite.config.ts:11` and import `describe`/`it`/`expect`/`vi` explicitly in tests. Adoption cost is moderate: the second option touches all 21 test files (mechanical, one import line each) and would require dropping `"vitest/globals"` from `types` in the same commit. Severity is Low because no production file currently does this — the finding is that nothing prevents it.

$ npx eslint --print-config src/lib/storage/repo.ts  ->  no-undef  [0,{"typeof":false}]
findings.verifierNote: Every load-bearing claim re-verified independently. tsconfig.json:17 is `"types": ["vite/client", "vitest/globals", "@testing-library/jest-dom"]` and :19 is `"include": ["src", "vite.config.ts"]` - one program spanning production and test files. node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts opens with `declare global {` and publishes `suite`, `test`, `describe`, `it`, `expect`, `assert`, `vitest`, `vi`, `beforeAll`, `afterAll`, `beforeEach` as ambient `let` bindings, so those identifiers are in scope for every file in the program, production included. I also re-ran the ESLint backstop check: `npx eslint --print-config src/lib/storage/repo.ts` reports `no-undef: [0, {"typeof": false}]`, so nothing catches a stray `vi.fn()` in a production module - it would typecheck, lint clean, and fail only in the browser as `vi is not defined`, inside the shipped bundle. `low` is right because no production file currently does this; the finding is that nothing prevents it.
findings.reachability: Latent by construction: the hole is open on all 65 non-test source files. No current production file references a test global (verified by the clean typecheck plus the fact that the app runs).
findings.blastRadius: Whole program. The remediation touches 21 test files (one import line each) or adds one tsconfig.test.json.
findings.suggestedPatch: Lowest-churn option: keep `globals: true` for the test runner but scope the ambient types - drop `"vitest/globals"` and `"@testing-library/jest-dom"` from tsconfig.json:17, add a `tsconfig.test.json` that extends the root, re-adds those two entries and sets `"include": ["src/**/*.test.ts", "src/**/*.test.tsx", "src/test/**"]`, and point the `typecheck` script at both. Risk: the two programs overlap on the files each test imports, so keep `skipLibCheck` and expect slightly slower typecheck; the alternative (drop `globals: true` from vite.config.ts:11 and import explicitly) is mechanical but touches all 21 test files and must land in the same commit.

findings.title: `HTMLMediaElement.duration` enters state as a plain `number` that can be `NaN` or `Infinity`, and is then both formatted and truthiness-tested
findings.description: `duration` is media metadata decoded by the browser — external data crossing into typed code with no validation. `HTMLMediaElement.duration` is `NaN` when unknown and `Infinity` for streams or containers without a duration header, and `number` claims neither is possible. Two consequences downstream: `formatTime(duration)` (line 217) computes `Math.floor(Infinity / 60)` and `Infinity % 60`, rendering the literal string "Infinity:NaN" in the transport bar (and "NaN:NaN" for NaN); and `max={duration || 100}` (line 212) uses a truthiness test on a number, which cannot distinguish "duration is genuinely 0" from "duration is unknown" — both silently become a 100-second scrubber whose thumb position is meaningless. Severity is Low because the app's only audio source is a locally generated WAV blob, whose header carries a finite duration, so the bad values are not reachable on the current happy path. Fix shape: validate at the assignment — `Number.isFinite(d) ? d : 0` — and use an explicit `duration: number | null` so "unknown" is a state the renderer must handle rather than a magic falsy number. Adjacent observation, filed here only for context because rejection handling belongs to the error-recovery audit: `togglePlay` (line 50) discards the `Promise<void>` from `.play()`, and `setIsPlaying(!isPlaying)` on line 52 flips the UI optimistically — if `play()` rejects (autoplay policy, or an AbortError when `src` changes), neither a `play` nor a `pause` event fires, so the button shows Pause over silent audio until the user clicks twice.
findings.verifierNote: Lines confirmed: AudioPlayer.tsx:62-66 `handleLoadedMetadata` -> `setDuration(audioRef.current.duration)`, :212 `max={duration || 100}`, :217 `{formatTime(duration)}` with `formatTime` at :97-101 (`Math.floor(time / 60)` / `Math.floor(time % 60)`), and `duration` initialised `0` at :21. The arithmetic claims are right - `Infinity` renders 'Infinity:NaN' and `NaN` renders 'NaN:NaN'. Two corrections drive the amendment. First, the `boundary-without-validation` framing overstates it: `HTMLMediaElement.duration` really is declared `number` in lib.dom.d.ts and TypeScript has no type that excludes `NaN`/`Infinity` from `number`, so nothing was weakened, bypassed, or asserted here - the defensible spec category is `js-implicit-coercion`, which the `max={duration || 100}` truthiness test at :212 matches exactly ('truthy checks that misbehave on 0'). Second, reachability is nil today, as the finding itself says: the only producer is `setActiveAudioTrack` (AppShell.tsx:82) fed by locally generated WAV blobs whose headers carry a finite duration. Severity `low` is correct; the adjacent `play()`-promise observation is correctly flagged as belonging to the error-recovery audit.
findings.reachability: Not reachable on the current happy path - the app's only audio source is a locally generated WAV. `duration` would need to be NaN/Infinity at `loadedmetadata`, which requires a stream or a container with no duration header.
findings.blastRadius: 1 component, 3 lines (:64, :212, :217). `AudioTrack.src` has 2 producers (BookDetail.tsx, EReader.tsx) both routed through AppShell.tsx:201.
findings.suggestedPatch: AudioPlayer.tsx:64 -> `const value = audioRef.current.duration; setDuration(Number.isFinite(value) ? value : 0);` and :212 -> `max={duration > 0 ? duration : 100}`. Risk: none - both are behaviour-preserving for finite durations; the fuller `duration: number | null` remodelling would additionally touch :21, :212 and :217 and is not needed to close the coercion.
findings.amendedDescription: `max={duration || 100}` (AudioPlayer.tsx:212) is a truthiness test on a number, so 'the track is genuinely 0s' and 'the duration is not known' both collapse to a meaningless 100-second scrubber - the spec's js-implicit-coercion pattern. The related weakness is that `duration` enters state unguarded at :64 from `HTMLMediaElement.duration`, which is `NaN` when unknown and `Infinity` for stream-like media, so `formatTime(duration)` at :217 would render the literal 'Infinity:NaN' or 'NaN:NaN'. This is a missing runtime guard rather than a bypassed type - TypeScript's `number` cannot exclude NaN or Infinity, so no assertion or `any` is involved - and it is unreachable today because the app's only audio source is a locally generated WAV with a finite duration header.

findings.title: reviewCards read path loads every row unvalidated and sorts on dueAt with a string method
findings.description: listByProfile and listByBook call `getAll('reviewCards')` - fetching every card of every profile - and immediately access `card.profileId` / `card.bookId` on rows typed only by db.ts:12-16. listDue then does `card.dueAt <= cutoff` and `a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt)` at line 89: a non-string dueAt makes the comparison at line 88 silently false (the card never becomes due, so it disappears from the review queue with no error) and, if it survives the filter, makes localeCompare throw. Note the cross-profile read also means one profile's corrupt card can break another profile's review session. Blast radius: 10 reviewCards.* call sites; the review queue is the whole of the Phase 3 feature. Correct behaviour: validate dueAt as an ISO string at the boundary, and prefer the existing 'by-profile-due' index over an unvalidated full-table scan.
findings.verifierNote: Pattern present: repo.ts:78-81 listByProfile does `getAll('reviewCards')` then reads `card.profileId`, repo.ts:94-97 listByBook does the same for bookId, and listDue at repo.ts:84-90 filters on `card.dueAt <= cutoff` (line 88) and sorts with `a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt)` (line 89) on rows typed only by the declaration at db.ts:12-16. Two of Discovery's claims do not survive. First, there is no ingress: the only writers to the reviewCards store are QuizModal.tsx:52 and useReviewQueue.ts:38, both routed through srs.ts, and both newCard (srs.ts:33) and scheduleCard (srs.ts:52) set dueAt from `new Date(...).toISOString()`. Neither the legacy migration nor the backup import touches reviewCards — so unlike summaries (F113) or profiles (F103) no non-string dueAt can arrive without direct database tampering. Second, the cross-profile claim is wrong: listDue calls listByProfile (line 86), which filters by profileId at line 80 before the comparison at 88-89, so another profile's row never reaches localeCompare. The full-table-scan vs by-profile-due-index point is a performance observation, which the spec places out of scope. Downgrading to low.
findings.reachability: No producer path can write a malformed card. Reaching the throw requires hand-editing IndexedDB or a future writer that bypasses srs.ts.
findings.blastRadius: Recounted excluding tests: 4 call sites — QuizModal.tsx:49, QuizModal.tsx:52, useReviewQueue.ts:20, useReviewQueue.ts:38 (plus repo-internal removeByBook at repo.ts:106). Discovery's '10' counted tests and repo-internal uses.
findings.suggestedPatch: Cheap defensive guard at repo.ts:88: `.filter((card) => typeof card.dueAt === 'string' && card.dueAt <= cutoff)`, so a tampered row drops out of the queue instead of throwing in the sort. Risk: it silently hides a corrupt record — pair it with a console.warn so the row stays attributable.
findings.amendedDescription: reviewCards.listByProfile/listByBook (repo.ts:78-81, 94-97) load every row unvalidated and listDue (repo.ts:88-89) then relies on dueAt being an ISO string for both the `<=` comparison and localeCompare. The declared type is unchecked, but the store has no external ingress: its only writers are QuizModal.tsx:52 and useReviewQueue.ts:38, both routed through srs.ts, which always writes `new Date(...).toISOString()`. No migration or import path writes review cards, and listDue filters by profileId before comparing, so a corrupt row cannot cross profiles. Hygiene-grade.

findings.title: The 200-book scale test hand-builds rows and bypasses parseGoodreadsCsv, the only validation in the feature
findings.description: The 'imports a large library without any AI cost' test constructs 200 objects `{ title, author, status: 'Want to Read' as const, rating: 0 }` and passes them straight to api.importGoodreadsRows. They satisfy GoodreadsRow structurally only because isbn13 and dateRead are optional (goodreads.ts:8-9), so the fixture never crosses the parser -- the single place in the feature where junk could be rejected. The result is that the parser -> importer seam is only ever exercised with the 2 well-formed rows of the CSV literal, while the only scale coverage runs on pre-sanitised data. Two consequences go untested: (a) the ISBN branch, since all 200 rows omit isbn13 so `coverForIsbn(undefined)` (goodreads.ts:121-122) returns undefined and every book falls to `placeholderCover(title)` -- the openlibrary cover URL path is covered by exactly one row; (b) the dedupe key `title.trim().toLowerCase()|author.trim().toLowerCase()` (useLibrary.tsx:132-133), which is trivially satisfied by 200 distinct titles all authored 'Someone' -- no test covers rows whose titles differ only by case, whitespace or a trailing series suffix, which is the realistic duplicate shape in a real export. importGoodreadsRows also declares no validation of its own on the GoodreadsRow[] it accepts.
findings.verifierNote: No type weakness exists here. The 200-row fixture at goodreadsImport.test.tsx:101-106 contains no cast: `status: 'Want to Read' as const` is literal-type narrowing (the opposite of a bypass), and `isbn13` / `dateRead` are declared optional at goodreads.ts:7-8, so omitting them makes the fixture a genuinely valid `GoodreadsRow` - not a lying fixture missing required fields. `importGoodreadsRows(rows: GoodreadsRow[])` (useLibrary.tsx:128-129) receives in-test literals, not external data, so the category boundary-without-validation ('external data typed as T via assertion or any') does not apply: nothing crosses a boundary in this test. Bypassing parseGoodreadsCsv in a test whose stated subject is 'imports a large library without any AI cost' is correct unit-test scoping, not a defect - and the parser IS exercised by the file's other three tests at :44, :65 and :88. The residual claims (the title|author dedupe key at useLibrary.tsx:132-133 untested for case/whitespace variants; the openlibrary ISBN branch at goodreads.ts:121-122 covered by one row) are accurate but are pure test-coverage observations with no type-system component, and belong to a coverage audit rather than this one.
findings.reachability: N/A - no defect.
findings.blastRadius: None.

findings.title: Cover lookups declare `Promise<string | null>` but can also reject — the signature lies to new callers
findings.description:
Both exported lookups declare a total contract over `string | null` (src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:1 and src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts:1), but neither is total: `fetch` rejects on any network failure, `response.json()` throws on a non-JSON 200 body, and `url.replace` throws if the L12 cast is wrong (see L06-F01). The declared return type advertises exactly two outcomes when there are three. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: either catch internally and genuinely return `string | null`, or make the throwing contract explicit in the signature/JSDoc so callers cannot miss it.

WHY IT MATTERS: the rejection path is real and proven — src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:53-61 stubs `fetch` to throw and asserts the placeholder fallback. Today the only caller, `fetchCover` (src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-20), wraps both in try/catch, so nothing breaks. But both functions are `export`ed from their modules, and a new caller reading `Promise<string | null>` has no type-level reason to wrap them — the compiler will happily accept `const url = await fetchGoogleBooksCover(t, a); if (url) ...` with no catch, and that call site rejects on the first offline user.

VERIFIED POSITIVE for contrast: the aggregate `fetchCover` in src/lib/covers/index.ts:12 IS honest — it declares `Promise<string>` and genuinely always resolves to a string because L21 falls through to `placeholderCover`. Its caller-side handling is also complete (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 handles the `string | undefined` from `coverForIsbn` with `??`). So the ambiguity is confined to the two provider modules.

BLAST RADIUS: 2 exported functions, 1 current caller each; the risk is entirely forward-looking (new call sites).
findings.verifierNote: The claimed type weakness does not exist. src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:1 and src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts:1 both declare `Promise<string | null>`, and that type is ACCURATE for every value either function ever resolves with: googleBooks returns `url.replace(...)` at :24 or `null` at :28; openLibrary returns a template string or `null` at :8. TypeScript's `Promise<T>` parameter describes the fulfilment value only - the language has no checked exceptions and no way to express rejection in a return type - so 'the signature lies' is a claim about a guarantee the type never made and that no TypeScript signature can make. Under this rule every fetch-calling function in every TS codebase is a finding. Verification criterion 4 also fails outright: there is no achievable replacement. The finding's own suggested fix ('catch internally and genuinely return string | null') would break the design the suite pins - src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:53-61 stubs fetch to throw and asserts `fetchCover` falls through to `placeholderCover`, which works only because the provider functions propagate. The alternative fix ('make it explicit in JSDoc') is prose, not type safety. Two further defects in the finding: the category `js-ambiguous-return` is defined by the spec as JavaScript-only and these are .ts files under `strict: true`; and the one concrete throw it names (`url.replace` on a non-string) is already counted as F085. Nothing survives that is not either inexpressible or double-counted.
findings.reachability: n/a. The only scenario is a hypothetical future caller writing `const url = await fetchGoogleBooksCover(t, a); if (url) ...` with no catch. The existing sole caller, src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-19, already wraps both in try/catch.
findings.blastRadius: 2 exported functions, 1 caller each - both reached only through `fetchCover` (src/lib/covers/index.ts:13). `fetchCover` itself has 2 non-test callers (src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:53, src/lib/ai/recommend.ts:37).

findings.title: DialogProps.size is a raw string interpolated into className, and no test ever passes a non-default value
findings.description: DialogProps declares `size?: string` (Dialog.tsx:11-12) for what is really a closed set of Tailwind max-width classes, and Dialog.tsx:35 interpolates it directly into the panel's className. Every render in this suite (lines 11, 64, 88) omits `size`, so the only value ever exercised is the 'max-w-xl' default. Two production callers pass real values that no test covers: ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38 (`size="max-w-lg"`) and ConfirmDialog.tsx:43 (`size="max-w-md"`). Because the parameter is a bare string, a typo ('max-w-x1'), a class Tailwind will purge, or an unrelated utility class all compile and silently render a full-width panel with no visual regression signal. Fix shape: narrow to a union of the permitted classes (or a semantic 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' mapped internally), which turns every typo into a compile error and makes the closed set self-documenting.
findings.verifierNote: The cited line contains no type weakness. Dialog.test.tsx:11 is `<Dialog open title="Add a book" onClose={onClose}>` inside the Harness — an omitted optional prop, not an assertion, an any, or a lying fixture (the spec's 'lying types in test fixtures are high-value' note applies to fixtures that assert an incomplete shape as complete; nothing is asserted here). The actual defect the finding describes — `size?: string` at Dialog.tsx:11-12 interpolated into className at Dialog.tsx:35 — is on the producer file and is already counted as F123 in this same batch, with the same two call sites (ConfirmDialog.tsx:43, ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38) and the same fix. What is left over is 'no test exercises a non-default size', which is a test-coverage observation, outside this audit's scope and not a duplicate-worthy finding on its own. Refuted as a test-side mirror of F123.
findings.reachability: n/a — no defect at the cited location.
findings.blastRadius: 0 independent of F123.

findings.title: The subscribe/emit store shape is hand-rolled twice, byte-identically, in `toastStore.ts` and `lib/ai/apiKey.ts`
findings.description: Both modules implement the same `useSyncExternalStore` backing store with the same three declarations copy-pasted: `const listeners = new Set<() => void>()`, an `emit()` that iterates it, and a `subscribeTo*(listener: () => void): () => void` that adds and returns a remover. The types are correct in both (no `Function`, no `unknown` payload, no untyped listener — see the verified negatives), so this is a duplication finding, not a soundness one: two sources of truth for one contract, and any future change (e.g. adding an unsubscribe-idempotency guard or a snapshot-version counter for `useSyncExternalStore` tearing) has to be made in two places or they drift. A single `createStore<T>()` returning `{ getSnapshot, subscribe, emit }` collapses both and makes the snapshot type a parameter rather than a per-module convention. Effort is trivial and the risk is low because both call sites already consume it through `useSyncExternalStore`. Blast radius: 2 modules, 2 React consumers (Toast.tsx:19 and the API-key hook).
findings.verifierNote: Read both files in full. The duplication is real (toastStore.ts:10 `const listeners = new Set<() => void>()`, :12-14 `emit()`, :39-44 `subscribeToToasts`; apiKey.ts:3 `listeners`, :5-7 `notify()`, :30-35 `subscribeToApiKey`) but it is not a type-safety defect and does not meet the spec's definition of `generic-opportunity` ('duplicated TYPE DEFINITIONS across modules that could collapse to a single generic'). Zero type definitions are duplicated: the only shared type is the builtin `() => void`, and toastStore's sole declared type (`ToastMessage`, :3-7) has no counterpart in apiKey.ts. The proposed `createStore<T>` has no `T` to bind on the apiKey side, because apiKey.ts holds no snapshot state at all - `getApiKey()` (:9-12) reads `localStorage` on every call, so there is nothing for `useSyncExternalStore` to snapshot except a derived value. What actually overlaps is a listener Set plus a 1-line for-loop, ~6 lines total across 2 modules; extracting a generic store for that is the speculative abstraction the project's own rules forbid. The finding's own text concedes 'the types are correct in both... this is a duplication finding, not a soundness one'.
findings.reachability: n/a - no unsound value can flow through either module; both are fully type-correct and there is no assertion, `any`, or suppression at either site.
findings.blastRadius: 2 modules, ~6 duplicated implementation lines, 0 duplicated type declarations, 2 React consumers.

findings.title: Two non-null assertions on array indexing that are no-ops today and would become the only unguarded spots if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` were enabled
findings.description: `items` is `HTMLElement[]` from `Array.from`, and with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: false` (tsconfig.json has `strict: true` but not this flag) `items[0]` is already typed `HTMLElement` — so both `!` are currently no-ops that the compiler ignores. They are still worth recording for two reasons. First, they are inconsistent with line 26 of the same file, which handles the identical "first focusable element" access with `?.` instead — two idioms for one question in twelve lines. Second, they are pre-emptive: if the project later enables `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (the single highest-value remaining strictness flag for this codebase — L12-F04's out-of-bounds quiz index and L12-F14's Record access are both instances of what it catches), these two lines will keep compiling silently while every other array access in the repo is forced to prove itself. The guard on line 45 does make them true today, so this is Low with no runtime failure. Fix shape: destructure with a length check, or use `at(0)`/`at(-1)` and handle `undefined`, so no assertion is needed either before or after the flag flips.
findings.verifierNote: Both assertions are present (useFocusTrap.ts:47 `const first = items[0]!;`, :48 `const last = items[items.length - 1]!;`) but they are correct as written and the proposed fix does not improve them. Line 45 (`if (items.length === 0) return;`) proves both accesses in-range, which the established baseline already records. Under the current tsconfig (`strict: true`, no `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) they are no-ops; under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` they would become load-bearing and STILL correct - and TypeScript has no control-flow analysis that can narrow `items[items.length - 1]`, so the suggested alternatives do not remove the assertion: `items.at(-1)` returns `HTMLElement | undefined` and `const [first] = items` is likewise `HTMLElement | undefined`. The 'inconsistent with line 26' argument does not hold either: `focusable()[0]?.focus()` at :26 sits in a scope with no length guard and makes a single optional call, so `?.` is the right idiom there and `!` is the right idiom here. A guarded, provably-true non-null assertion is not what the `non-null-assertion` category targets ('crashes at runtime if the assumption is wrong' - this assumption cannot be wrong).
findings.reachability: Tab-key handler at :36-58; reached on every Tab press inside a modal. The assertions are exercised constantly and are always true because of :45.
findings.blastRadius: 2 assertions, 1 file, 0 call sites depend on them (both are function-local).

findings.title: AiError.kind carries the full union on every instance, so MissingKeyError does not narrow its own tag and per-kind payloads have nowhere to live
findings.description: `AiErrorKind` is a well-formed string-literal union and `kind` is the natural discriminant, but it is declared as the whole union on the base class, so no subclass refines it: `new MissingKeyError().kind` types as the full eight-member `AiErrorKind` even though it is unconditionally `'missing-key'`. The immediate cost is small and honest to state — `src/app/AppShell.tsx:49` (`aiError.kind === 'missing-key' || aiError.kind === 'invalid-key'`) is the only consumer that branches on the tag, and TypeScript would still flag a renamed member there as a no-overlap comparison, so the tag is not currently unsafe. The structural cost is that the union cannot carry per-kind data: `rate-limited` has a `retryDelay` in Google's RetryInfo detail and `invalid-key` has an HTTP status, but `AiError` can only stash them in `cause: unknown` (line 15), which no consumer in the repo reads. That is what forces the fix for L04-F01 to go through re-parsing rather than through the type. Correct shape: make `kind` a type parameter or declare `readonly kind: 'missing-key'` on `MissingKeyError`, and if per-kind data is ever needed, model `AiError` as a discriminated union over `kind` with a payload per member rather than a single class with an untyped `cause`. Blast radius: 1 branching consumer (AppShell.tsx:49), 1 subclass (MissingKeyError, constructed at client.ts:11), 2 test files.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present as described (errors.ts:13 `readonly kind: AiErrorKind` as a base-class parameter property; MissingKeyError at :22-26 always passes 'missing-key') but it is the correct type at every existing consumer, and the spec's bar for a discriminated-union finding - a concrete call site where a wrong value could arrive and compile - is not met. I grepped every consumer: the only tag branch in the repo is AppShell.tsx:49 `if (aiError.kind === 'missing-key' || aiError.kind === 'invalid-key')`, and the value it inspects comes from `toAiError(error)` (errors.ts:45), whose declared return is the BASE `AiError` - so the full union is genuinely the right type there and refining a subclass would change nothing. The only subclass is `MissingKeyError`, constructed once at client.ts:11 and immediately `throw`n, so its static type is erased at the catch; there is no site where narrowing is wanted and unavailable. TypeScript already rejects a renamed member at :49 as a no-overlap comparison, which the finding concedes. The remaining argument - that per-kind payloads have nowhere to live except `cause: unknown` - is explicitly conditional ('if per-kind data is ever needed') and no consumer in src/ reads `cause`; recommending a class-to-union restructure for a payload nobody consumes is speculative design, not a defect.
findings.reachability: Every AI failure flows through `toAiError` -> `AiError` -> AppShell.tsx:49. The union-typed tag is exercised constantly and behaves correctly.
findings.blastRadius: 1 branching consumer (AppShell.tsx:49), 1 subclass (client.ts:11), 2 test files. No production value is mis-typed.

findings.title: Summary.model is a bare string, so nothing type-checks that a persisted model id is a real one
findings.description: `model: string` records which Gemini model produced a summary, with `'legacy'` as a documented sentinel for migrated rows. `src/lib/ai/models.ts` already declares `MODELS` with `as const`, so the exact union `(typeof MODELS)[keyof typeof MODELS] | 'legacy'` is available at zero cost. As typed, any string is accepted: a typo'd or hand-edited model id round-trips through the store unnoticed, and — relevant to the project's stated invariant that model IDs live only in `src/lib/ai/models.ts` — nothing stops a literal model id being written from elsewhere, which is exactly what `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:131` does with `model: 'legacy'`. Impact is low today because the field is currently only recorded, not dispatched on; it becomes a real problem the moment any code branches on it or a model is renamed and stale ids need finding. Correct shape: narrow the field to the union derived from `MODELS` plus the `'legacy'` sentinel, which makes a Google model rename a compile error at every stale write site rather than a silent data inconsistency.
findings.verifierNote: The pattern is present (types.ts:64 `model: string`, with the doc comment at :63 naming 'legacy' as the migration sentinel) but the recommended narrowing would introduce the very defect this audit exists to find, so this should not be actioned. `Summary.model` is a PERSISTED HISTORICAL PROVENANCE field: it records which model produced a stored summary, and models.ts's own comment says 'A Google rename is a one-line change here'. The moment that rename happens, every already-persisted summary in IndexedDB still carries the OLD id - which would no longer be a member of `(typeof MODELS)[keyof typeof MODELS] | 'legacy'`. Narrowing the field therefore makes the declared type false about the data on the read path, i.e. a lying type, which is strictly worse than the current honest `string`. The branded-type bar is also not met: I grepped every write (chat.ts:14, quiz.ts:11, recommend.ts:25, summarize.ts:39/47/63/89, tts.ts:19 all pass `MODELS.*` to the SDK, not to this field; the only writes to `Summary.model` are summarize.ts's own value, migrate.ts:131 `'legacy'`, and three test fixtures) and there is no read anywhere in src/ - so there is no call site where a wrong value could arrive and be consumed, and no adjacent same-typed parameter to swap it with. The project invariant 'model IDs live only in src/lib/ai/models.ts' is about where IDs are AUTHORED, which migrate.ts:131 does not violate ('legacy' is not a model id).
findings.reachability: Written on every summary generation and on migration; read by nothing in src/. No branch depends on the value.
findings.blastRadius: 1 field, 3 production writers, 0 readers, 3 test fixtures (useLibrary.test.tsx:95, markdown.test.ts:28, repo.test.ts:77) which the proposed narrowing would break.
